source_passage: No. 21 is another one of the larger and more elegant buildings in the place, with eight arcades. It was given to Cardinal Richelieu by Henri IV, but no one knows for sure if he ever lived here. [...] He bequeathed the building to his grand-nephew, who then passed it on to his son. The son never lived here either, but he is rumored to have made good use of his pied-à-terre to get to know almost every woman in the place. This hôtel was restored in the summer of 1978. [...] They went to the brickworks in Versailles, which had made the original bricks in the seventeenth century, and they matched the missing parts as closely as possible. [...] Look closely at the sides of the arcade pillars right above the pediments and you will find little square stone patches. These patches date from the Revolution, when this section of the arcade was used as a forge for making arms. The patches cover the points from which metal curtains were hung to close off the forge. [...] Until around 1930 the arcades were filled with shops of all kinds—butchers, shoemakers, and so on—and each shop walled itself in by setting beams into cuts in the stone.

script_body: Look at the heavy wooden door of no. 23, decorated with thick wooden plaques attached by metal bolts. Inside, the small garden and vaulted brick entry belong to the Hôtel de Marie-Charlotte de Balzac d'Entragues — a woman whose career more than matched her name. She lived here with her mother, who had been the mistress of Charles IX; her sister Henriette had been the mistress of Henri IV. Decidedly these ladies did not bring good luck to their lovers. Marie-Charlotte was the mistress of the maréchal de Bassompierre and bore him a son, Louis, in 1610. When he refused to marry her despite a written promise, she consoled herself with a string of distinguished replacements: the archbishop of Paris Jean-François de Gondi, and the financier Le Plessis-Guénégaud among them.

Small garden and vaulted brick entry inside the courtyard

script_body: The restaurant Guirlande de Julie at no. 25 is named for a small seventeenth-century book of madrigals — each poem surrounded by a different flower — that the Duc de Montausier offered his wife on May 22, 1641. It's owned, like Coconnas at no. 2, by Claude Terrail of the Tour d'Argent. Look up at the right side of no. 25: the large hemisphere of glass on the ground floor usually marks a shop, but this is a private home, and the owners let the window serve as their view of the square.

It's an identical twin of the Pavillon du Roi except for two details: the Médicis sun emblem on its façade, and an unusually long iron balcony. The small street at the back, the rue de Béarn, was the exit route for every parade that passed through the place Royale.

script_body: No. 24, the Hôtel du Maréchal de Géran, is less illustrious than its neighbours, but it did have one notorious resident: the wife of Duc de Boufflers, maréchal of France. She was fourteen when she married, and quickly became famous for her beauty, caustic wit, and number of lovers. A contemporary verse caught her reputation: "Quand Boufflers parut à cour, / On crut voir la mère d'amour, / Chacun s'empressait à lui plaire / Et chacun l'avait à son tour." (When Boufflers appeared at court, / You would have thought you were looking at Venus; / Everyone tried to please her / And everyone had her in turn.)

trigger_address: no. 6 rue du Pas de la Mule
script_body: A short walk out of the square east, at no. 6 rue du Pas de la Mule, is one of the most fascinating shops in Paris — called the Boucherie, the butcher's shop. Above the door, the old meat hooks still hang. The walls are original tile. M. Bissonet comes from a long line of butchers, but his passion for musical instruments slowly won out: first he hung violins and trumpets alongside the sausages, then the meat vanished. His cold-storage room is now a library of music books. He's shown visitors a silver-etched guitar, a porcelain trumpet, a tuba of Venetian glass — and played a Breton bombardon only twelve inches long that makes an enormous sound. If he's in, he might play something for you.

source_passage: Walk east out of the place, to no. 6 rue du Pas de la Mule. This is one of the most fascinating shops in Paris. It was called the Boucherie (butcher's shop), but it now sells musical instruments. Note above the doorway the metal hooks from which meat was once hung. The tiled walls are original. M. Bissonet comes from a long line of butchers, and this shop was his until his passion for musical instruments gradually won out. He began by hanging violins and trumpets alongside his sausages, but eventually the meat vanished [...]. His cold-storage room has become a library of books on the topic [...]. He showed us a silver-etched guitar, a porcelain trumpet, and a tuba made of Venetian glass. He also played for us a Breton bombardon, a flutelike instrument that is only twelve inches long [...].

script_body: Press the button above the keypad at no. 20 and step into the courtyard. The front wall has been paused mid-restoration for twenty-five years. An architect who specialised in prefabricated building wanted to recase the façade in hollow brick; the authorities objected that the original was plaster painted to resemble brick. The decision: status quo. So the ugly glass balcony and the partially-completed seventeenth-century façade stay exactly as you see them — and give you the best look anywhere in the square at the colombage technique, where large cornerstones frame the wall and small stones and rubble are bound together with plaster.

physical_cues.cue: Exposed wall at no. 20 showing the colombage technique — large cornerstones framing small stones and rubble filled with plaster
Partially-completed glass balcony, construction halted twenty-five years ago

inline_foreign_phrases.gloss: timber-framing construction technique

source_passage: Press the button above the keypad at no. 20 to enter the courtyard, and face the front wall (facing the place). The wall is in the midst of repairs that were halted twenty-five years ago. [...] The architect's plan here was to build a new facade in the original seventeenth-century style that would encompass the hallways and incorporate them into the building. He began construction with hollow bricks, but when the authorities found out, they objected, saying that the original did not have bricks at all but rather plaster painted to resemble bricks. The decision? The building must remain in status quo, that is, the ugly glass balcony and the partially completed work would have to remain as they were. [...] Look at the window frames on the right and left of this wall as well as at the corners. You can see how the large stones were used as a frame, which was then filled in with small stones and rubble and covered with plaster. This is essentially the same colombage technique used in the sixteenth century.

source_attribution.author: Sonia Landes, Alison Landes, Rebecca Landes

script_body: No. 18 was the hôtel of Marguerite de Béthune, Duchesse de Rohan, daughter of Sully, Henri IV's first minister. She was married at nine, in 1604, had innumerable lovers — many of them neighbours on this square — and of her nine children, only one daughter survived her. In the stairwell on the left you can see a bronze statue of a gypsy girl; she's missing the lantern from her left hand and one earring. The concierge will tell you, proudly, that Victor Hugo put her there, though we've never found that in writing. What we do know is that the gypsy was stolen some years ago. A resident called the police and got immediate results — she was found minutes later at a nearby traffic light, her head sticking out of the back of a pickup truck. She's now firmly bolted to her red-marble base, which is firmly bolted to the floor.

script_body: No. 16 was owned in the seventeenth century by a royal counsellor named François le Roux, who had the dubious distinction of marrying "une petite garce qui se donnait pour un quart d'écu" — a little bitch who gave herself for a quarter of an écu. That was slightly less than a livre, but in those days a livre was a day's wages for a manual worker, so Mme le Roux was not so cheap after all. Today the courtyard needs restoration, but step in to see the wrought-iron railing on the left and the mascarons over the portal and entry.

script_body: No. 14 — the Hôtel de l'Abbé de la Rivière — is now one of the best-restored hôtels in the square, its six arcades redone in real brick and its wrought-iron balconies cleaned of rust. It's a synagogue today. The half facing the place serves the Ashkenazic community (eastern-European, mostly Yiddish-speaking); the half on the rue des Tournelles serves the Sephardic (Jews who settled in Spain and Portugal, now largely from North Africa). When the doors on the place are unlocked, Friday evenings and Saturday mornings, step inside to see wood-panelled walls, stairs carpeted with Oriental rugs, plants in the entry — the interior of a Victorian home, because that's exactly what it was: the chief rabbi of France once lived here with his wife and five children. The hôtel takes its name from a seventeenth-century owner, the Abbé de la Rivière, favourite of the Duc d'Orléans — a tailor's son who rose to duke and bishop of Langres, though he never quite made cardinal. The best painters of the era, Le Brun and Mignard, decorated his ceilings. Those ceilings are preserved today in the Musée Carnavalet.

script_body: The Musée Victor Hugo at no. 6 was Hugo's residence from 1832 to 1848 — until his disagreements with Louis Napoléon sent him into political exile on Guernsey. The museum is free; the top floor gives you Hugo's life, the second his drawings and mementos, the first a re-creation of his apartment, with each room dedicated to a period of his life. Don't miss the restored bedroom with his Louis-XIII deathbed and his death mask, or the striking Chinese-style dining room with its bright red chimney, which he built himself during his Guernsey exile. Before Hugo's time this was the hôtel of the Princesse de Guéménée — Anne de Montbazon — the most famous précieuse of the place. She was married at twelve, and like other premature wives of the day never settled into monogamy. Her lovers read like a guillotine list: the Comte de Montmorency-Bouteville, beheaded 1627 for his famous duel; Henri II of Montmorency, beheaded 1632; the Comte de Soissons, dead 1641; Auguste de Thou, beheaded 1642. She brought no luck to her lovers, but she herself lived to be eighty-one. The property stretched back to no. 17 rue des Tournelles with a discreet rear alley for quick exits — a feature Hugo himself often used when visiting his own mistresses. Before you leave the museum, look out of a second-floor window: from that height, above the trees, you can see the whole square.

script_body: Marion Delorme may also have lived in a small pavilion at the back of no. 6, though most historians doubt she and Anne de Guéménée could have shared the same house peaceably — the traffic alone would have caused jams. Marion was Anne's equal in lovers and in the brilliance of her salon. She began as courtesan to Jacques Vallée — a notorious epicurean and avowed atheist — moved on to the handsome Marquis de Cinq-Mars, who plotted against Richelieu and lost his head for it (Alfred de Vigny's novel Cinq-Mars is about him). Then George Villiers, the first Duke of Buckingham, whom you may remember from The Three Musketeers. Then Louis II de Bourbon, Prince de Condé — the great Condé — who imprisoned his own wife on faked charges and wrote to the king asking she never be released. Nice fellow. Marion is said, finally, to have got Cardinal Richelieu himself into her bed — which neatly keeps everything in the family, since Condé's unfortunate wife was Richelieu's niece. Victor Hugo wrote a drama about her; Bottesini an opera.

physical_cues.cue: Façade of no. 6 place des Vosges

source_passage: Marion Delorme may also have lived here, in a small pavilion at the back [...]. Marion was a match for Anne in every way, in number of lovers and in the brilliance of her salon. She began her career as courtesan to Jacques Vallée, sieur Desbarreaux, a notorious 'epicurean' (read: hedonist) and, unforgivable at the time, an avowed atheist. Next came the Marquis de Cinq-Mars, a handsome, stylish courtier who made the mistake of plotting intrigue against Richelieu and lost his head. (The marquis may have died young, but his place in history and literature is assured as the protagonist of Alfred de Vigny's novel Cinq-Mars.) After the execution of Cinq-Mars, Marion is said to have gone on to a long series of lovers, including George Villiers, the first Duke of Buckingham. (You may remember him from The Three Musketeers.) Also Louis II de Bourbon, Prince de Condé (called 'the great Condé') [...]. Yet this great wencher had his own wife confined for her alleged unfaithfulness [...] and wrote his last letter to the king to ask that she never be released. Nice fellow. Last but not least, Marion is said to have gotten Cardinal Richelieu himself into her bed. [...] Victor Hugo wrote a drama called Marion Delorme, and G. Bottesini wrote an opera of the same name.

source_attribution.author: Sonia Landes, Alison Landes, Rebecca Landes

script_body: Restaurant Coconnas at no. 2 (its front door actually opens on the rue de Birague around the corner) is owned by Claude Terrail of the Tour d'Argent. Both of Terrail's places appear in the film Who Is Killing the Great Chefs of Europe? The specialty here is poule-au-pot — stewed chicken — a menu that quietly commemorates Henri IV's famous promise of "a chicken in every pot."

script_body: For nearly a thousand years a prison called Le Grand-Chatelet stood here on Place du Chatelet, demolished only between 1802 and 1808. It began in the year 870 as a wooden tower built by Charles le Chauve to defend the Pont au Change against the Norsemen; in 1130 Louis VI replaced it with a proper fortress, superseded in turn by Philippe-Auguste's city walls in 1190, after which the Châtelet became the main Paris courts, the provostship, and the prison. The 16th-century poet Clément Marot was locked up here for the offence of eating meat during Lent, and named the poem he wrote afterward L'Enfer — Hell. Today's only visible trace is a plan of the prison engraved in marble on the façade of the Chambre des Notaires at 12 avenue Victoria, unnoticed by most passers-by.

source_passage: Few connect it with the ghastly prison of Le Grand Chatelet, which stood here for nearly a thousand years and was only demolished between 1802 and 1808. A plan of the Grand-Chatelet is engraved in marble on the facade of the Chambre des Notaires at 12 avenue Victoria, unnoticed by most passers-by. In 870 Charles le Chauve erected a primitive wooden tower in front of the bridge (Pont au Change) to defend it against the Norsemen; it seems to have played its role effectively. Around the year 1130 Louis VI built a proper fortress to protect the Ile de la Cité [...]. The city walls erected by Philippe-Auguste in 1190 made this fortress superfluous and it therefore became the seat of the Paris courts of law, provostship and main prison. [...] the agony of its prisoners can be perceived through the lines of 16th century poet Clément Marot, who was locked up here for having eaten meat on Lent and who named his poem, significantly L'Enfer (Hell).

script_body: The fountain in the centre of the square, La Victoire, was erected in 1808 to commemorate Napoleon's Egyptian campaigns. When he returned, Paris was seized by an Egyptomania that sent the city scrambling to adorn its streets with pseudo-Egyptian art — hence the four crouching sphinxes flanked to each side of the fountain's socle.

source_passage: In its centre the fountain La Victoire, erected in 1808, commemorates Napoleon's Egyptian campaigns, following which Paris was seized by a feverish Egyptomania and set out to adorn her streets with pseudo-Egyptian art. Hence the four crouching sphinxes flanked to each side of its socle.

script_body: Before Haussmann, this area was a maze of dark alleys north of the square with names like rue de la Tuerie — Carnage — and rue de l'Ecorcherie — Skinning. It was the realm of cut-throats and felons, and more threateningly to Napoleon III, a lair of political opponents and rioters. Haussmann reduced it to ashes and cut Boulevard Sébastopol through it, giving the government forces clean lines of sight over any future crowd. While he was at it he turned the new square into a fashionable neighbourhood: Davioud's two theatres went up in the 1860s, and the Théâtre du Châtelet was inaugurated in 1862 with a magical performance of Around the World in Eighty Days. The fashionable set never quite came. The neighbourhood later found its place in the opening lines of T.S. Eliot's Wasteland.

source_passage: The Théatre du Chatelet (Théatre Musical de Paris or TMP) and the Théatre de la Ville on either side of the square were later additions by Davioud built in the 1860s, when the present square was opened as part of the Second Empire's scheme to rehabilitate what was hitherto a seedy slum. [...] Another maze of dark alleys lay north of the square, the realm of cut-throats, villains and felons; even more threateningly to the authorities — a lair of political opponents and rioters, which determined Napoleon III's right-hand man, the Baron Haussmann, to reduce it to ashes. The broad artery of Boulevard Sébastopol replaced it [...]. Hence the new square and its two elegant theatres and the pompous inauguration of the Théatre du Chatelet in 1862, with a magical performance of Around the World in Eighty Days. But the neighbourhood never attracted the fashionable set. Rather, it was a source of inspiration to the opening lines of T.S. Eliot's Wasteland.

script_body: For generations of French provincials between the 1860s and the 1960s, the name Châtelet meant not the prison or the metro junction but the Théâtre du Châtelet — the highlight of a visit to the capital, specialising in sugary operettas like L'Auberge du Cheval Blanc, The White Horse Inn. Luis Mariano was the adulated star, sweeping the ladies off their feet with his schmaltzy Mexico.

script_body: The quai takes its name from the mégissiers — tanners — who worked here for hundreds of years, slaughtering lambs and fowl and wreaking havoc on the Seine. Louis XIV eventually ruled them out of the city and transferred them to the remote banks of the Bièvre in the southern 5th and 13th arrondissements, where they caused just as much damage, but out of his sight.

script_body: The Palais de Justice stands on the site of the first residence of the kings of France — and before them, the Roman governors of Lutetia. In 360 the Roman general Julian, the future emperor Julian the Apostate, was proclaimed emperor on this spot by his own soldiers. Part of the Roman palace was still standing when Clovis and the first Merovingian kings returned to the site in the 6th century, and the second dynasty — Pépin le Bref, Charlemagne, Louis le Débonnaire, Charles le Chauve — lived here too, until the Norman invasion of the 9th century destroyed everything and reconstruction had to begin again from the ruins.

physical_cues.cue: 18th-century wrought-iron gate at the entrance, the Palais de Justice behind it

source_passage: the Palais de Justice, on the site of the first residence of the kings of France, and before them of the Roman governors. Above all Julian who in 360 was proclaimed here emperor by his soldiers. Part of the Roman palace was still standing when the Merovingian kings (the first French dynasty) returned to the site in the 6th century. It is not quite clear whether Clovis, the founder of the dynasty, lived here, but all his followers did, throughout the 7th century. There is also evidence of the presence of the Carolingian kings (the second dynasty) - Pépin le Bref, Charlemagne, Louis le Débonnaire, Charles le Chauve. With the Norman invasion in the 9th century came total destruction.

script_body: The moat and drawbridge that defended this palace proved useless on 22 February 1357. Jean II le Bon, of the Valois dynasty, was being held captive in England. The provost of merchants, Etienne Marcel, thought he could overthrow the monarchy with English help. That afternoon the young Dauphin — the future Charles V — was sitting in the palace with two of his counsellors when Marcel's men burst in and slew the counsellors before his eyes. The Dauphin was unhurt, but the victims' gushing blood stained his clothes, an experience he never forgot. A prudent politician, deservedly called le Sage — the Wise — he slipped out of the palace one night by way of the river, moved to the remote Hôtel de Saint-Pol in the Marais, and arranged for himself a new residence within the safer walls of the Louvre, where he spent time from 1368 onward. The kings of France never returned to the island.

source_passage: These did not prove sufficient during the bloody revolt led by the provost of merchants, Etienne Marcel in 1357. With Jean II le Bon, the founder of the Valois dynasty, held captive in England, and reckoning on the support of the English, Etienne Marcel believed he could overthrow the monarchy. On 22 February the Dauphin (the future Charles V) was sitting with two of his counsellors when the provost's men erupted into the palace and slew his counsellors before his very eyes. The Dauphin was unhurt, but the gushing blood of the victims stained his clothes, an experience he was not going to forget. A prudent politician, deservedly known as le Sage, he left the palace one night stealthily by way of the river and moved to the more remote Hôtel de Saint-Pol in the Marais, meanwhile arranging for himself a residence within the safer walls of the Louvre, where he spent time from 1368 on. The kings of France never returned to the island.

The House of Valois was founded by Charles, Count of Valois (d.1325); the first Valois KING was Philip VI (1328); Jean II le Bon was Philip VI's son (the second Valois king). Strike the false 'founder of the Valois dynasty' epithet — e.g. write 'Jean II le Bon, of the Valois dynasty' (drop 'founder'). Keep the rest ('held captive in England') unchanged.

script_body: The Sainte-Chapelle was built by Saint Louis to house a piece of the Holy Cross and the Crown of Thorns, which he bought from Baudouin II, the last Emperor of Constantinople, who was in desperate need of funds to defend his city. The architects — Pierre de Montreuil, or perhaps Jean de Chelles — were set an unusual brief: design a chapel to have the light, lacy aspect of a reliquary. The result was stunningly beyond expectation. It took barely five years. The silver and gold reliquary that originally held the Crown of Thorns was sent to the Mint during the Revolution, but its contents — genuine or not — miraculously survived and are kept today at Notre-Dame. Even the standard-bearers of the Revolutionary ideal, it seems, did not dare to tamper with the most holy of Christian symbols. The chapel itself was shown no such consideration: it served as a flour store, then as a depot for court archives, growing so dilapidated that in 1847 it still bore an inscription reading 'National property, for sale.' Fortunately enlightened souls called on Viollet-le-Duc, Lassus, and others to restore the church, and 720 of the 1,134 original stained-glass scenes were preserved.

He had bought them from Baudouin II, the last Emperor of Constantinople, who was in desperate need of funds to defend his city. The chapel was therefore designed to have the light, lacy aspect of a reliquary. The result was stunningly beyond expectation. It took its architect (Pierre de Montreuil or, perhaps, Jean de Chelles) barely five years to build a masterpiece of harmonious proportions [...]. Although the silver and gold reliquary containing the crown of thorns was dispatched to the Mint during the Revolution, its contents (whether genuine or not) have miraculously survived and are now kept at Notre-Dame. Is it that even the standard-bearers of the Revolutionary ideal did not dare to tamper with the most holy of Christian symbols? The chapel was not shown the same consideration and was used first to store flour, then as a depot for the court house archives; by which time it was so dilapidated that it was put on the market for sale and demolition. In 1847 it still bore an inscription which read: 'National property, for sale'. Fortunately, some enlightened souls [...] called upon Viollet-le-Duc, Lassus and other artists to restore the church to its ancient beauty. [...] 720 of the 1,134 original scenes having been preserved.

script_body: On 24 May 1871, barely four years after the full restoration was complete, the Communards poured petrol over the Sainte-Chapelle and only failed to set it on fire for lack of time. Everything you see inside is what they almost burned.

script_body: In the 15th century passers-by could still hear the screams of tortured prisoners from the Tour Bonbec — the westernmost tower of the Conciergerie. During the tower's restoration in 1828, workers found two oubliettes in the basement: concealed dungeons spiked with iron points and connected to the river. Needless to dwell on the fate of the prisoners dropped into them. The name bon-bec — medieval French for prate — probably alluded to the interrogations on the ground floor, where a varied spectrum of torture methods was devised to extract confessions and denunciations.

During its restoration in 1828, two oubliettes, communicating with the river and spiked with iron points, were found in its basement: needless to dwell on the fate of the prisoners. The name bon-bec ('prate' in the Middle Ages) probably alluded to the interrogations that took place on the ground floor: a varied spectrum of torture methods was devised to make the victim confess and denounce his accomplices.

script_body: Among the notorious prisoners held here in later centuries were Ravaillac — the assassin of Henri IV — the mass poisoner La Marquise de Brinvilliers, who had eliminated the better part of her own household, and Cartouche (1693–1721), the most notorious bandit of his age. To be admitted into Cartouche's gang you had to prove yourself an expert cutpurse: candidates practised on dummies hung with little bells, and had to strip the dummies without the slightest tinkling. All three awaited execution here.

source_passage: Among the notorious prisoners of the Conciergerie in later years were Ravaillac, the assassin of Henri IV; the mass poisoner La Marquise de Brinvilliers (1630-1676), who had eliminated the better part of her numerous household; and Cartouche (1693-1721), the most notorious bandit of his age, the terror of Paris. In order to be admitted into his prestigious gang one had to be proved an expert cutpurse. Candidates were made to practise on dummies covered with little bells, until they could strip them without the slightest tinkling. All three prisoners awaited execution at the Conciergerie.

script_body: During the Revolution the Conciergerie boasted an impressive list of prisoners awaiting their deaths. Madame Roland, who had supported the Revolution but sided with the Girondins at the wrong moment. Marie-Antoinette, who occupied a dreary cell from 2 August to 16 October 1793, until she was taken to the guillotine on the Place de la Révolution — today's Place de la Concorde. Later Danton, Robespierre, and Saint-Just were detained here in turn, Danton and Robespierre occupying the cells adjacent to the Queen's. Today one visits for French history, but the Gothic halls and kitchen fireplaces deserve to be visited for their architectural merit as well.

Today one visits the Conciergerie for the sake of French history, but the impressive Gothic halls and kitchen fire-places deserve to be visited for their architectural merit.

script_body: North of the Gothic halls ran a section of the prison leading to the dark cells, known as rue de Paris — named after the Great Executioner, Monsieur de Paris. That post was held by seven successive generations of the Sanson family, from 1688 to 1847, transmitted from father to son. Shortly before the Revolution, Louis XVI had set his heart on improving the executioners' plight and granted Charles-Henri Sanson an annual fee of 16,000 pounds plus 2,000 crowns for the upkeep of the scaffold and pillory — never suspecting he would become his own executioner. Being a royalist, Charles-Henri had no desire to carry out that deed. On 15 August 1792 he was arrested as "the despot's employee"; with each execution he was dispatched from his cell to the Place du Carrousel, where the guillotine then stood, and afterwards taken back. Early on executions were few, but once the guillotine began to work at full swing and his expert hand could not be spared, he was released. He retired soon after he had executed his sovereign. His son Henri held the position through the Terror and the precarious regimes that followed, until 1840 — well into the reign of Louis-Philippe.

Shortly before the Revolution Louis XVI had set his heart on improving their plight and granted Charles-Henri Sanson an annual fee of 16,000 pounds plus 2,000 crowns for the upkeep of the scaffold and pillory, undoubting he would become his own executioner! Being a royalist, Charles-Henri had no desire to carry out that deed. script_body: The film-maker Jean Renoir marvelled that his own grandfather — the painter Renoir's father, a tailor from Limoges — had known Henri Sanson's chief assistant during the Terror. The old assistant, Renoir wrote, "may have passed Voltaire and Benjamin Franklin in the street, heard Mozart play the harpsichord, and attended performances of Monsieur Beaumarchais." Old Renoir met him in 1845, the year the family had moved up to Paris from Limoges and when the last Sanson still held the post. The two became friends — the tailor and the executioner's assistant — united by the pleasure of doing a good job. "After all," Jean Renoir observed, "they were two good workmen: one cut out cloth, the other cut off heads just as conscientiously."

script_body: Place Dauphine was created by Henri IV in 1607 in honour of his son the Dauphin, the future Louis XIII, and enclosed on all sides by arcaded brick-and-stone houses — like its contemporary, the Place des Vosges in the Marais. The location was deliberate: bankers and tradesmen could conduct their business undisturbed, a few steps from the Louvre. In the 18th century, talented young artists not yet admitted to the official Salons were allowed to hold an annual exhibition here. Today the business and the art trade have moved elsewhere, and the square has become a quiet, provincial-feeling nest of boutiques and pretty eating-places — a haven of peace in the heart of Paris.

source_passage: You will reach the triangular Place Dauphine, one of Paris's romantic gems. Created by Henri IV in 1607 in honour of his son the Dauphin and future Louis XIII, it was enclosed on all sides by arcaded brick-and-stone houses, similarly to its contemporary Place des Vosges in the Marais. Bankers and tradesmen could carry on their negotiations undisturbed, on a site conveniently located only a few steps away from the Louvre. In the 18th century talented young artists, unable as yet to exhibit in the official Salons, were given an opportunity to hold an annual exhibition here. Today both business transactions and the art trade have moved to other parts and Place Dauphine is a haven of peace surrounded by small boutiques and pretty eating-places, a provincial nest in the heart of Paris.

script_body: The garden at the tip of the island, the Square du Vert-Galant, sits just below Henri IV's equestrian statue on the Pont-Neuf. The nickname Vert-Galant — the Green Gallant — honours the king's famously amorous career. From the garden, the view of the Hôtel de la Monnaie and the dome of the Institut de France on the left, the Louvre on the right, and the Pont-des-Arts ahead is unforgettable. By night the square is an enchantment.

script_body: In 1190, before leaving on the Third Crusade, Philippe-Auguste ringed the right bank with a three-thousand-metre wall — three metres thick, ten metres high — and anchored it on the west with a fortress at the river's edge, facing the Tour de Nesle opposite. He had reason to worry: the Plantagenets sat just downstream in Normandy, and within living memory the Norsemen had invaded Paris the same way. His brother-in-law Richard the Lionheart, companion on the holy journey to Jerusalem, was no more reliable than the rest. At the heart of the new fortification rose a round keep, nineteen metres in diameter, thirty-one metres above ground — the first Louvre. On his return in 1191 he deposited the Crown treasures and archives here, deeming it the safest place in Paris — "la plus halte tor de Paris la citet," the tallest tower in Paris the city.

source_passage: Initially it was no more than a defence tower, part of the fortification system that Philippe-Auguste had built in 1190 round the part of Paris that lay north of the Seine [...]. Wary of a potential threat from England by way of the Seine, albeit upstream (which is how the Norsemen had invaded the city three centuries earlier), he erected the Louvre on the right bank [...]. With the presence of the Plantagenets not so far down the river [...], and with the vague memory of that horrendous devastation of Paris by the Norsemen, he had good reason for concern: [...] Richard the Lionheart [...] was his brother-in-law and was to accompany him on his holy journey to Jerusalem. Soon a wall 3,000 metres long, 3 metres thick and 10 metres high encircled the right bank [...]. Inside, a round keep, 19 metres in diameter, rose 31 metres above ground level - the initial Louvre. Upon his return in 1191, Philippe-Auguste deposited the Crown treasures and archives at the Louvre [...], 'la plus halte tor de Paris la citet' ('the tallest tower in Paris the city').

script_body: Charles V, though equally dedicated to fortifying his capital, was an enlightened king. Besides making the Louvre his residence in 1368, he collected within its thick walls the kingdom's manuscripts and founded the first royal library of France — the seed from which two centuries later the greatest painting collection in the world would grow.

script_body: François I, settling into a new period of peace and refinement, decided to dispense with the defensive function of the Louvre and replace the medieval fortress with a Renaissance palace. The people of Paris were quite upset by the sudden disappearance in 1528 of la Grosse Tour — the Big Tower — where Charles V used to read and meditate. For François, however, fortresses carried unpleasant associations: he had recently been released from the fortress of Madrid, where Emperor Charles V of Spain had kept him captive after defeating him at Pavia in 1525. His overhauled Louvre was meant to be the opposite of a prison — a sumptuous backdrop for tournaments and jousts, where in 1540 he dazzled the same Emperor Charles V during his state visit.

source_passage: François I, settling into a new period of peace, well being and refinement, decided to dispense with the defensive function of the Louvre and replaced the medieval fortress with a Renaissance palace [...]. The people of Paris were quite upset by the sudden disappearance in 1528 of 'la Grosse Tour', where Charles V used to read and meditate. For François I, however, fortresses had unpleasant associations: he had recently been released from the fortress of Madrid where he had been kept captive by the Emperor Charles V, who had defeated him at Pavia in 1525.

script_body: François I's painting collection was embryonic — works by Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael, Titian — but it was the seed of today's two-thousand-odd masterpieces. The Mona Lisa, the most renowned of them all, is believed to have been brought to Paris from Amboise in the Loire Valley after Leonardo's death there in 1519.
source_passage: he also started the painting collection that would one day make it the largest painting museum in the world. His was but an embryonic collection, comprising, nonetheless, the works of such great masters as Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael, Titian, among them, and probably, the most renowned painting in the Louvre, the Mona Lisa, which François I is believed to have transferred to Paris from Amboise (in the Loire Valley) after the death of da Vinci in 1519.

script_body: In 1593, four years after his accession, Henri IV bartered his Protestant religion for Paris to end the bloody strife between Protestants and Catholics — "Paris vaut bien une messe," Paris is well worth a mass. Paris meant first and foremost the Louvre. Catherine de Medici had built the Palais des Tuileries facing the Louvre in 1564, to the west, running north–south along the Seine. Henri IV set out to connect the two palaces with a colossal wing of monumental grandeur — La Grande Galerie, four hundred and sixty metres long, also known as the Galerie du Bord de l'Eau because it ran along the water's edge. It met the Tuileries at right angles and was capped with the elegant Pavillon de Flore. The enterprise was a constant headache for his minister Sully, who had to squeeze segments of the population dry to raise the funds.

script_body: Louis XIV was fourteen when he settled in the Louvre in 1652, after the princely rebellion — la Fronde — had been quelled and it was deemed safe for him to return to Paris. He never liked the Louvre and in 1682 moved his court to the newly-built palace at Versailles, leaving the Louvre to fall into decline. But as long as he resided here, he channelled enormous energy and money into completing the construction around the Cour Carrée; the show had to go on, and to exceed in flashy splendour that of his predecessors. His was the reign of glamour par excellence. Scintillating balls, ceremonial dinners of twenty dishes, then performances of Corneille and Molière — His Majesty and his brother Monsieur were great lovers of theatre, unlike their grandfather Henri IV, who once confided to a woman friend: "Yesterday evening I saw the comedians play, when I fell asleep. It was midnight when they finished." During this reign the painting collection went from two hundred to two thousand pieces, largely thanks to his minister Mazarin's feverish acquisitions and Colbert's patronage — bolstered, before his disgrace, by ample donations from Nicolas Fouquet, the king's wealthy treasurer.

source_passage: Louis XIV was 14 when he settled in the Louvre in 1652, after the princely rebellion - la Fronde - had been quelled [...]. He never liked the Louvre and in 1682 moved his court to the newly built palace at Versailles, leaving the Louvre to fall into decline. However, as long as he resided there, he channelled a lot of energy and money into completing the construction around the Cour Carrée [...]. Scintillating balls, ceremonial dinners, each consisting of a score of dishes, were succeeded by performances of plays by Corneille and Molière. His Majesty and his brother, Monsieur, were great lovers of this form of entertainment, unlike their grandfather Henri IV, who once confided to a woman friend, "Yesterday evening I saw the comedians play, when I fell asleep. It was midnight when they finished." During the reign of Louis XIV the number of paintings in the Louvre increased from 200 to 2,000, thanks largely to his enterprising aides, particularly his minister Mazarin [...]. Mazarin's successor, Colbert, also encouraged the development of the arts and sciences, supported by ample donations made by Nicolas Fouquet, the king's wealthy treasurer, before his disgrace.

script_body: Once Louis XIV moved to Versailles, the Louvre fell to pieces. The King's vacant apartment became the premises of the Académie des Sciences, housing an elephant skeleton, a stuffed camel, and various anatomical organs floating in alcohol-filled jars. Booths and stalls crammed the courtyard. The magnificent halls were devastated, the panelling of the royal apartments torn off, the painted ceilings drilled through to make room for skylights and stove pipes. A motley population of artisans, parasitical courtiers, and prowlers replaced the splendid members of the court who had moved to Versailles — reluctantly in many cases, resentful at having to give up the independence they had enjoyed in the city.
source_passage: The King's apartment, for example, left vacant when he moved to Versailles, became the premises of the Académie des Sciences, housing an elephant skeleton, a stuffed camel and various anatomical organs floating in alcohol-filled jars. Worse was to come: booths and stalls soon crammed the courtyard, the magnificent halls were devastated, the panelling of the royal apartments torn off, the painted ceilings drilled into to make room for skylights or stove pipes. A motley population of artisans, parasitical courtiers and prowlers replaced the splendid members of the court who had moved to Versailles. Many courtiers had gone reluctantly, resentful at having to give up the independence they had enjoyed in the city.

script_body: On 6 October 1789 the infuriated people of Paris marched Louis XIV's great-great-grandson, Louis XVI, back from Versailles to the Tuileries — the Louvre being by then too dilapidated to inhabit. A long, strange procession escorted the royal coach: National Guards, royal troops, Parisian crowds, and carts of corn and flour watched over by sharp-eyed mutinous women. From that day the Tuileries replaced the Louvre as the residence of French monarchs. After his 1851 coup Louis Napoleon promptly abandoned the Republican Palais de l'Élysée for the royal Tuileries. In 1871 the Commune burned it; the infant Third Republic, victorious, refused to restore the charred carcass. In 1882 it razed the palace to the ground, "securing irrevocably," as Vallois puts it, "the definitive death of the monarchy."

physical_cues.cue: Eastern end of the Tuileries gardens — where the Palais des Tuileries stood until 1882, now an open view to the Louvre

source_passage: Roughly a century after the move to Versailles, on 6 October 1789, the infuriated people of Paris transferred Louis XIV's great-great-grandson, Louis XVI, back to Paris. [...] Heading from Versailles to the Tuileries (the Louvre being too dilapidated to be inhabited), the royal coach was made to follow a long and strange procession of National Guards, royal troops, excited throngs of Parisians and carts of corn and flour escorted by sharp-eyed mutinous women. From then on the Tuileries replaced the Louvre as the residence of the kings and emperors of France. This explains why, after his coup on 2 December 1851, Louis Napoleon promptly left the Republican seat of the Palais de l'Élysée [...] in favour of the Royal seat of the Tuileries. [...] The fire that had damaged the Tuileries during the civil strife of the Commune, had tolled the knell of the 1st arrondissement as the seat of power. In 1882, rather than restore the charred carcass of the Palais des Tuileries, the Third Republic razed it to the ground, securing irrevocably the definitive death of the monarchy.

script_body: When the Tuileries was still the seat of power, the ladies of the Napoleonic nobility drew an English clientele to this stretch of rue de Rivoli: the prestigious Meurice at no. 228 faced the Tuileries Gardens, the English bookshop Galignani at 224 kept the daily papers of home, and WH Smith opened its Paris branch at 248 for their convenience. The jewellery and clothes shops of rue de Castiglione and Place Vendôme catered to the same set. It was here, serving Empress Eugénie and the other ladies of the Napoleonic court, that French haute couture was born in the second half of the 19th century — pioneered by Charles Worth, the Empress's English couturier. A century later its centre of gravity drifted westward to the 8th arrondissement.

script_body: The regal rue Saint-Denis was the "Champs-Élysées" of medieval Paris — the sacred way by which royal processions entered the capital. Kings returning from coronation at Reims passed through here on their way to Notre-Dame; and at the other end of a reign, it was along this same route that each king was carried to his final resting place in the basilica of Saint-Denis, north of the city. One street, bookending the life of every French monarch.

script_body: In 1135 Louis VI set up a primitive market here on a piece of land allotted by the Bishop of Paris, against a return of one-third of the revenue. The name — Les Champeaux, Little Fields — probably derived from the marshy market-gardens that surrounded it. You are standing on ground that has been a market for nearly nine hundred years.

script_body: In 1183 Philippe-Auguste replaced the wooden market with two stone buildings — sheltering goods from the weather, fitted with locks against thieves. To fund the work, he confiscated the possessions of the Jews of Paris.

script_body: The name stuck in its own colloquial wisdom: Les Halles, or les alles, "pour ce que chacun y allait" — for everyone went there.

source_passage: The new market became known as Les Halles, or les alles: 'pour ce que chacun y allait' ('for everyone went there'), and it was this name that stuck.

script_body: Henri II rebuilt the market in 1553; three centuries later, in the Industrial Age, Napoleon III repeated the move. Impressed by Victor Baltard's newly-built Gare de l'Est, the emperor commissioned him to rebuild Les Halles, commending iron over stone: "Faites-moi des parapluies!" Make me umbrellas! Fourteen iron pavilions went up between 1851 and 1857, and stood until 1969.

source_passage: Economic prosperity and demographic growth in the 16th century led Henri II to rebuild and enlarge the market in 1553, an initiative repeated by Napoleon III three centuries later [...]. Impressed by Victor Baltard's newly-built Gare de l'Est, Napoleon III commissioned him to build the new market, commending the use of iron: "Faites-moi des parapluies!" ("make me umbrellas!"). 14 iron pavilions were thus erected between 1851 and 1857 and stood till 1969.

script_body: In 1969 the central market was transferred to Rungis, south of Paris — deemed unsuitable for modern times. Many Parisians were appalled by the demolition of Victor Baltard's iron pavilions, considered an artistic testimony to the Industrial Age. Only one of the fourteen was allowed to survive, and even it was moved to the suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne. A surreal gigantic hole — "le trou des Halles" — replaced the belly of Paris, then left gaping for a decade while ambitious politicians shilly-shallied about its fate. In 1979 the Forum des Halles rose out of the ashes: the largest pedestrian precinct in Europe, a genuine achievement in a traffic-ridden city, but also — barely more than another shopping centre, 240 shops, generally gaudy. Sculptor Raymond Mason mourned: "Il est un lieu de bonheur... la dernière image du naturel dans la Ville. Il est maintenant le Paradis Perdu." Louis Chevalier, the Paris poet-historian, was blunter: "La mort des Halles a sonné le glas de Paris" — the death of Les Halles has tolled the knell of Paris.

In 1979 the Forum des Halles rose out of the ashes of the picturesque central market. [...] 240 [shops], and generally gaudy.

script_body: In 1873 Emile Zola gave Les Halles its most enduring nickname — "the belly of Paris" — as the title of his novel. He had spent a year haunting the market at all hours, recording the ever-changing hues of this gigantic digestive apparatus of the capital: bluish-grey metal structures against a light grey sky in wet weather; sheets of gold on the hard-packed earth when the sun broke through; the glowing glass panes of the pavilions at sunset; gas-lamp lights against black roofs at night. Poultry, fish in wicker baskets, meat, cheese, butter and milk each had its own pavilion. Bouquets of thyme, laurel and garlic lay in neat rows at the foot of Saint-Eustache, the aroma of Provence vying with the smell of carrots and celery. He watched les forts des Halles — the robust porters, "all nerves and muscles" — then descended into the underground where the nightly slaughter was done, reeking of blood and overrun by rats. Meanwhile, in the upper world, bourgeois and artists drifted in from cabarets and theatres in the early hours, looking for strong emotions, finishing the onion soup and glass of wine with a chunk of baguette dunked in a café crème to celebrate the new day. Evelyn Waugh ate exactly that same onion soup at Au Père Tranquille in 1929.

physical_cues.cue: Saint-Eustache just north of the gardens — the church Zola used as anchor for his descriptions of the thyme, laurel and garlic at dawn

source_passage: Emile Zola had dubbed its plebeian eastern parts 'the belly of Paris' a metaphor he used in 1873 for the title of one of his novels. For a year he had been haunting the central market of Les Halles at all times of day and night, imbibing the atmosphere and recording the ever-changing hues [...]: dark bluish-grey metal structures against a light grey sky in wet weather; sheets of gold on the hard-packed earth as the sun's rays penetrate through the grey atmosphere on a fine day; the glowing glass panes of the market's pavilions at sunset; the lights of gas lamps standing out against black roofs. Poultry, fish in wicker baskets, meat, cheese, butter and milk each had their own pavilion. [...] The smell of carrots, parsley and celery vie with the aroma of Provence - bouquets of thyme, laurel and garlic arrayed in neat rows at the foot of the church of Saint-Eustache. Having watched at work les forts des Halles - the robust porters, 'all nerves and muscles' - Zola descended into the undisclosable underground depths of the market, where the shameful slaughter of fowl and other creatures was carried out nightly, a place reeking of blood and pestilence and overrun by rats. [...] The onion soup and the glass of wine at the typical zinc bar would be followed at the break of dawn by a chunk of baguette dunked in a café crème [...]. where in 1929 Evelyn Waugh also dined on onion soup.

script_body: From the 14th century on, the scaffold was part of the landscape here. The King's pillory, largest of all the pillories in Paris, was a sizeable octagonal structure with a pointed roof and weathervane — resembling, oddly, a chapel. The Great Executioner often lived on the ground floor, while convicts were exposed in the tower above. The excited mob relished the sight, taunting the exposed victims and pelting them with rubbish. There were no gallows at Les Halles, however — the King conceded this was no place to leave bodies rotting on a rope.
source_passage: With its ceaseless human tide, the market-place was picked out for public executions and punishments and the scaffold was part of the landscape from the 14th century on. [...] the King's pillory, the largest of them all, was a sizeable octagonal structure, with a pointed roof and weathervane, somewhat resembling a chapel. The ground floor was often inhabited by the King's Great Executioner, while the convicts were exposed in the tower above. The excited mob relished the sight, taunting the exposed victims, pelting them with rubbish and litter. There were no gallows, however, at Les Halles, the King conceding that this was no place for bodies to be left rotting on a rope.

script_body: The notorious poissardes of Les Halles — the Dames des Halles — were on ceremonial occasions admitted into the King's Palace to pay their respects. They returned with Palace gossip, and the physical proximity of high and low bred a certain familiarity. On 30 August 1608, a market-woman named Femme Ladoucette wrote to Marie de Medici, Henri IV's second wife. She introduced herself as a Dame des Halles "from mother to daughter since Saint Louis" — and a mother of four by her husband (a guarantee of moral integrity) — and admitted to a forthright tongue, but, she added, not a lying one. She then complained about the Queen's philandering husband, the King — a good fellow deep down, but one who fidgets at the sight of a coquette and scatters bastards around despite being blessed with a most appetising Queen, so well conditioned to have little princes. If the King ever wandered through Les Halles, she wrote, she would give him a sound thrashing for the love of her Queen. Far from being scolded, Femme Ladoucette was promoted — fournisseuse royale, royal purveyor.

source_passage: On special occasions these notorious poissardes were allowed into the King's Palace to pay their respects to the royal couple. [...] The Dames des Halles [...] an astonishing letter, written by Femme Ladoucette to Marie de Medici, Henri IV's second wife, on 30 August 1608. Having introduced herself as Dame des Halles 'from mother to daughter since Saint Louis', and a mother to four by her husband (which is a guarantee of moral integrity), she admits to a forthright tongue, but, she adds, it is no lying tongue... She then proceeds to complain to the Queen about her philandering husband, the King, a good fellow deep down but who fidgets at the sight of a coquette and scatters bastards around, although blessed with a most appetising Queen, so well conditioned to have little princes. script_body: For centuries the Cimetière des Saints-Innocents piled up the remains of generations of Parisians on the corner of today's rue Berger and rue Saint-Denis, from Gallo-Roman days onward. By the late 18th century the stench of putrefaction and the risk of epidemics had grown so severe that a general outcry finally turned against the site. Voltaire called it a barbarity that placed the French below the Hottentots. One journalist, opposing the demolition on religious grounds, was sent to the Bastille for an entire year. Today the square bustles with street performers around a Renaissance fountain — most unaware they are treading the soil that once buried the innocent dead.

Renaissance fountain of the Innocents at today's Place Joachim Du Bellay

source_passage: The Cimetière des Saints-Innocents, into which had been piled up the remains of generations of Parisians since Gallo-Roman days, stood on the corner of rue Berger and rue Saint-Denis. By the late 18th century the stench of putrefaction and the danger of epidemics were so great that a general outcry arose, this time against the preservation of a site. Voltaire considered it a barbarity that placed the French below the Hottentots! But one journalist who opposed the demolition on religious grounds, was sent to the Bastille prison for an entire year. [...] Today, the Square des Innocents, now Place Joachim Du Bellay, bustles with street performers and loitering crowds, who gather around the Renaissance fountain with its cascading water, unaware that they are treading the soil that once buried the innocent dead.

script_body: The transfer of the cemetery's occupants to the newly opened catacombs south of the city — now in the 14th arrondissement — began on 7 April 1786 and took fifteen months. Night after night, eerie processions carried draped remains from the different cemeteries of Paris to their new abode. Six million rest there now.

script_body: Saint-Eustache is the second-largest church in Paris after Notre-Dame — an imposing, somewhat maternal 16th-century witness to the congregation of Les Halles. Louis XIII received his first communion here, Madame de Pompadour was baptised here, Cardinal Richelieu was baptised here. Jean-Baptiste Lully was married here. Jean-Philippe Rameau was buried here. The church survived the market above it, the cemetery beside it, and stands still, watching the traffic-free gardens where mothers and their young now gather.

[...] the names of the greats are also associated with this church, where Richelieu and Pompadour were baptized, Louis XIII received his first holy communion, Lully was married and Rameau was buried.

script_body: A plaque on the wall of the southern aisle records that the funeral service for Anna Maria Mozart was held here in July 1788. She had accompanied her son on his third and last visit to Paris. No longer the Wunderkind who had enchanted the courts of Europe, Mozart was ignored by a shallow, unmusical society and left Paris bereaved and embittered. His mother lay here.

script_body: The painter Auguste Renoir grew up in one of the slum lanes that then ran through the Esplanade of the Louvre. He was one of the street urchins to whom Queen Amélie's ladies-in-waiting threw sweets through the window when they made too much of a nuisance of themselves. Renoir's son Jean, the film director, later wondered "how successive kings could have tolerated such a seedy neighbourhood under their very noses."

Twenty-one scenes from Belle Époque Paris are on display in this wax museum, providing a kitschy and sketchy yet truly instructive idea of turn-of-the-century Paris and its representative figures - Victor Hugo, Emile Zola, Jules Verne, Pasteur etc. You will travel to the old village of Montmartre, to the fashionable Champs-Élysées, to the bustling market of Les Halles, obviously; you will admire the 1900 Universal Exposition and will be dazzled by the scintillating bourgeoisie at the Opera of Palais Garnier.

script_body: Mozart and his mother shared an insalubrious, draughty flat at no. 10 rue du Gros-Chenet — today's rue Sentier in the 2nd arrondissement. She took ill in June of 1788 and died wretchedly on 3 July. Mozart gives a heart-rending account of the event in his Correspondence. Resentful and contemptuous of Parisian society, he left the city the following September, never to return. The plaque you just saw on the southern aisle marks her funeral service held here.

script_body: Two famous funeral services were held here. Jean de La Fontaine's passed without incident. Molière's did not. It took the intervention of the king to persuade the Saint-Eustache clergy to give this parishioner a Christian burial — the clergy did not like "stage men" and did not admit them into its fold. The actors gave them good reason: those ill-mannered louts would turn up in front of the church during Sunday morning mass to announce their forthcoming play, inevitably more exciting than mass, thus turning many souls away from God.

All the more so because those ill-mannered louts would turn up in front of the church during Sunday morning mass to announce their forthcoming play - otherwise more exciting than mass - thus inevitably turning many souls away from God.

script_body: The church's remarkable acoustics drew the great composers. In 1855 Berlioz attended a performance of his uplifting Te Deum by nine hundred and fifty musicians. In 1886 Liszt's majestic Grand Mass was premiered here, also in the presence of its composer. The choir was directed by no other than Charles Gounod — whose most outstanding pupil was a child by the name of Auguste Renoir. Gounod had built great hopes in young Renoir, who, however, felt a deeper urge to use his hands.

source_passage: Because of its remarkable acoustics, the names of several illustrious musicians are associated with the church of Saint-Eustache. In 1855 Berlioz attended a performance of his uplifting Te Deum by 950 musicians and in 1886, Liszt's majestic Grand Mass was premiered here, also in the presence of its composer. The famous choir of Saint-Eustache was directed by no other than Charles Gounod, whose most outstanding pupil was a child by the name of Auguste Renoir. Gounod had built great hopes in young Renoir, who, however, felt a deeper urge to use his hands.

script_body: The church houses one of the most fabulous organs in Paris — the Dutch firm Peter Jan Van Den Heuvel installed it in 1989 inside a beautiful 19th-century case designed by Victor Baltard, the architect of Les Halles. The double-transmission mechanism — both mechanical and electronic — makes it the largest of its kind in the world. On your way out through the northern aisle, look for the colourful niche depicting the life of Les Halles — a tribute to the market's workers, the "good people of Paris."

script_body: At the Vidéothèque, the entire memory of Paris is preserved in video archives — fiction and documentary alike. The siting is pointed: it sits on the ground where the organic heart of Paris once beat. A viewer need only press a button and the city comes to life on the screen. Of late, private homes have had links installed to the Vidéothèque, sparing the owners the bother of going outside — while disconnecting them from the real city around them.

source_passage: You could spend endless days at the Vidéothèque where the entire memory of Paris is preserved in video archives (both fiction and documentary), appropriately situated on the site where the organic heart of Paris once beat. To experience this vicariously, the viewer need only press a button and the city comes to life on the screen. Of late, private homes have had links installed to the Vidéothèque, sparing the owners the bother of going out, while at the same time disconnecting them from their real environment.

script_body: Next to the Vidéothèque is another world of visual illusion. At the Parc Océanique Cousteau, video has replaced both the ocean's waters and its creatures — the fish spared from languishing in boredom in an artificial environment by the simple expedient of not being there at all. Exorbitant admission fees fund the Cousteau Society's quality-of-life-on-our-planet work; the gift shop next door continues the same cause.

source_passage: Next to the Vidéothèque, le Parc Océanique Cousteau is yet another world of visual illusion. In this gigantic aquarium, the video has replaced both the ocean's waters and its creatures so as to prevent the fish languishing in boredom in an artificial environment. The expensive technology entailed accounts, perhaps, for the exorbitant admission fees. The receipts, however, are used for the protection and improvement of the quality of life on our planet. The gift shop next door is run by the Cousteau Society, for the same cause.

trigger_address: corner of rue des Prouvaires and 54 rue Saint-Honoré
script_body: Rue Saint-Honoré was a major artery in pre-Revolutionary days, leading to the Louvre and the Palais-Royal — but for a brief period it was the sinister route of the tumbrils, carrying the condemned from the Conciergerie prison to the guillotine on Place de la Révolution, today's Place de la Concorde. On 16 October 1793, the painter Jacques-Louis David posted himself on this corner balcony, 54 rue Saint-Honoré, and watched Marie-Antoinette carried to her doom — her hands tied behind her back. The tragic sight became his shattering portrait of the Queen.

source_passage: rue Saint-Honoré. A major artery in pre-Revolutionary days, leading to the Louvre and to the Palais-Royal, the street is still lined with 17th- and 18th-century houses. A close friend of the royal family, Fersen had tried to help them escape. Now, a quiet Paris shopfront — where the conspiracy bought its secrecy in a bottle.

script_body: At the corner of rue Vauvilliers, the first episode of the Fronde — the revolt against Louis XIV's mentor and minister Mazarin — began in August 1648. Just further down, at 2 rue Sauval, was the birthplace of Molière in 1622. The original house was later demolished and replaced by the one still standing today — where Richard Wagner stayed in 1839.

script_body: In the 13th century this street was the stronghold of the iron trade — narrow, congested, cluttered with blacksmiths' and ironmongers' stalls. It was still much the same on 14 May 1610, when the royal coach was held up here with the King aboard, on his way from the Louvre to the Arsenal near the Bastille where his minister Sully was residing. The King was absorbed in a letter. A man named Ravaillac jumped onto the coach and stabbed him. The assassin was declared mentally deranged but was nevertheless sentenced to be quartered on Place de Grève — today's Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville — a sentence speedily carried out thirteen days after the crime. The King had been rushed to 93 rue Saint-Honoré, where an earlier apothecary was trading, but he could not be saved.

script_body: Henri IV's early amorous adventures had earned him the affectionate nickname of le Vert Galant — the amorous youth. The charm faded as he grew older. The population resented his dozens of bastard children scattered through the kingdom, which all but plunged France in civil strife again. Worse, he had expressed his intention to marry his favourite, Gabrielle d'Estrées — an outrage to the raison d'état. Only her premature death prevented the infamy. As Femme Ladoucette had written to the Queen, in the kingdom of France one separated the sheep from the goats.

source_passage: This was not the first murder attempt made on the life of the King; for while his early amorous adventures had gained him the affectionate nickname of le Vert Galant (the amorous youth), the charm faded as he grew older. The population resented the fact that he had dozens of bastard children scattered throughout the kingdom, which all but plunged France in civil strife yet again. Furthermore, he had expressed his intention to marry his favourite, Gabrielle - an outrage to the raison d'état. Only the latter's premature death prevented this infamy. In the kingdom of France, as Femme Ladoucette had expressed it in her letter to the Queen, one separated the sheep from the goats.

script_body: The Fontaine des Innocents — the only Renaissance fountain in Paris — was designed by Pierre Lescot and sculpted by Jean Goujon in 1549. Goujon was the greatest sculptor of his time. The fountain was inaugurated on 16 June 1549 for Henri II's solemn entry into Paris. It originally had three arcades and a balcony, where prominent figures sheltered during royal processions.

The fountain had three arcades and a balcony at the time, where prominent figures took shelter during royal processions. script_body: The fountain has moved. It originally stood at the corner of rue Saint-Denis and today's rue Berger, against the church of Saints-Innocents which was demolished when the cemetery closed down. A colourful fruit, vegetable, and herb market replaced the cemetery in 1787. That market was demolished in 1855, and the fountain was shifted, altered, and restored a couple of times before it settled here at Place Joachim Du Bellay.

script_body: Ernest Cognacq, a former draper's assistant from La Rochelle, set up shop on rue du Pont-Neuf in 1867. He called it La Samaritaine after the old water pump that had stood at the Pont-Neuf until the early 19th century. Thirty years later he commissioned Frantz Jourdain to put up a full-scale department store in steel and glass. In 1926 Jourdain and Henri Sauvage added the Art Deco façade on quai du Louvre, one of the best in Paris. With his dynamic wife Louise Jay — also a draper's assistant, from rue Rambuteau — Cognacq turned his success into a fabulous art collection, now the Musée Cognacq-Jay in the Marais. The old catch-phrase, "On trouve tout à la Samaritaine," has lately been sharpened to "On trouve Tout-Paris à la Samaritaine" — a showbiz polish for a shop whose shoppers remain notoriously provincial.

Thirty years later he commissioned Frantz Jourdain to put up a building to house a full-size department store, a structure of steel and glass [...]. script_body: At the stroke of midnight on 24 August 1572, one of the bloodiest pages in French history began here. The massacre of Saint-Bartholomew, ordered by Charles IX but instigated by his mother Catherine de Medici, left three thousand Protestants dead. Three bells had signalled the onset of the carnage — Marie, Germain, and Vincent. Only Marie has survived. She dates from 1527, one of the oldest bells in Paris, and she still rings from above your head. This was the royal parish church, just opposite the Louvre; the royal pew can still be seen inside.

physical_cues.cue: The bell Marie, cast in 1527, still hanging in the belfry — one of the oldest bells in Paris
Royal pew still visible inside — this was the royal parish church, opposite the Louvre

source_passage: On 24 August 1572, at the stroke of midnight, began one of the bloodiest pages in French history: the massacre of Saint-Bartholomew, ordered by Charles IX but instigated by his mother Catherine de Medici, during which 3,000 Protestants perished. Of the three bells that had signalled the onset of the carnage - Marie, Germain and Vincent, only Marie has survived. It dates from 1527 and is one of the oldest bells in Paris. Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois was the royal parish church, just opposite the Louvre, and the royal pew can still be seen inside.

script_body: Catherine de Medici's astrologer Ruggieri warned her she would die "by Saint-Germain." She took the prophecy literally, moved out of her newly built Tuileries — west of this church — and stopped returning to her residence at Saint-Germain-en-Laye too. There is no escaping one's destiny. Sixteen years later, ill at Blois in the Loire Valley, she asked the young priest called to her bedside for the last sacrament on 15 January 1589 for his name. "Julien de Saint-Germain," replied the holy stranger.
source_passage: When Catherine de Medici was told by her astrologer, Ruggieri, that she would die 'by Saint-Germain', she moved out of the Palais des Tuileries, her newly built residence west of the Louvre, so as to attend mass elsewhere. [...] the queen never returned to her residence at Saint-Germain-en-Laye either, but there is no escaping one's destiny: while in Blois in the Loire Valley, some 16 years later, she took ill, never to recover. A young priest was called to her bedside on 15 January 1589 to give her the last sacrament. The Queen asked his name: 'Julien de Saint-Germain,' replied the holy stranger.

script_body: The rotunda was first built by Louis XVI as La Halle au Blé for the trade of corn, flour, and sugar; the present structure dates from 1889. Look at the elegant buildings lining the northern curve of the circular rue des Viarmes — they sit on Catherine de Medici's Hôtel de Soissons, where she had fled Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois after Ruggieri's prophecy. The tower from which her astrologer scrutinised the stars still stands, its graceful carving partly surviving. Ruggieri used the tower until the end of his life, and despite his unfavourable predictions, he never fell into disgrace — he had also, after all, correctly foretold the mortal injury of Henri II by Montgomery in 1559.

physical_cues.cue: Circular rue des Viarmes curving around the rotunda — traces the old Hôtel de Soissons footprint

source_passage: the Bourse de Commerce first built by Louis XVI for the trade of corn, flour and sugar and known as La Halle au Blé. The present rotunda dates only from 1889. The elegant buildings that line the northern curve of the circular rue des Viarmes deserve special mention. The tower of Catherine de Medici's residence was sculpted with exquisite grace, as you can surmise from what has survived. Ruggieri used the tower until the end of his life, and despite his unfavourable predictions, he never fell into disgrace. Before bringing the Queen unpleasant news about her own fate, he had already predicted her husband's mortal injury in single combat. Indeed, Henri II was mortally injured by Montgomery during a friendly tournament.

script_body: Véro and Dodat, the two charcutiers — pork butchers — who built this arcade in 1826, went bankrupt shortly after. The gas lights created quite a sensation; property prices rocketed; fashionable ladies in crinolines and gentlemen in top hats flocked through. In 1836 the celebrated actress Rachel moved into the third floor of no. 38. The ground floor housed the satirical paper Charivari, to which Daumier contributed his cartoons. And it was in Charivari that a journalist called Louis Leroy first coined the word "Impressionist" — he borrowed it from Claude Monet's painting Impression, soleil levant, and applied it derogatorily to the entire group of painters who were striving in vain to gain recognition from a stuffy, conformist public that considered them mentally deranged. With the age of the stagecoach, the Messageries Générales opened premises on rue du Bouloi on the other side of the arcade. The magical spell broke; the beau-monde migrated elsewhere. What is left is an oasis of nostalgia — and at no. 26, Robert Capia, world-renowned antique-dolls dealer.

source_passage: N° 19 opens on to a picturesque outdated arcade, overlooked by most contemporaries: la Galerie Véro-Dodat which will carry you nearly two centuries back. Its beautiful glass ceiling, its black-and-white chequered floor, its mahogany panelling, its brass framings and handles served as backdrop to the promenade of fair ladies in crinolines and gentlemen in tail-coats and top hats [...] when it opened in 1826. The arcade's gas lights created quite a sensation and prices of property rocketed. But somehow, Messieurs Véro and Dodat, the two charcutiers (pork butchers) who had built the arcade, went bankrupt. In 1836 the celebrated actress Rachel moved to the 3rd floor of n° 38. The ground floor of the house was occupied by the famous satirical paper Charivari, to which Daumier contributed his cartoons. It was in the Charivari that the word 'Impressionist' was first coined by a journalist called Leroy. He had borrowed it from Monet's painting Impression, soleil levant and applied it derogatorily to the entire group of painters [...]. With the age of the stagecoach, the Messageries Générales opened premises on rue du Bouloi, on the other side of the arcade. From then on, the place became a convenient shortcut for travellers and its magical spell was broken. The beau-monde migrated elsewhere. What is left is an oasis of nostalgia, charmingly antiquated shops, among them Robert Capia at n° 26, a world-renowned dealer in antique dolls.

script_body: François d'Aubusson, maréchal and Duc de La Feuillade, idolised his king. He decided to put up a statue of Louis XIV on his own property, at his own expense — covered all over in gold, adorned with His Majesty's court cloak, crowned with a laurel wreath. At his feet, four chained women represented his trampled enemies: Spain, Holland, Germany, Franche-Comté. This done, the preposterous Maréchal called on the genius of Jules Hardouin-Mansart to create a setting worthy of the object of his worship. The result was the elegant Place des Victoires. La Feuillade, by then the laughing stock of Paris, is said to have relieved the King when he finally gave up the ghost. The statue was melted down during the Revolution; Bosio replaced it during the Restoration — this time Louis XIV sits on a caracoling horse, dressed as a Roman emperor, but still wearing his wig.

physical_cues.cue: Bosio's equestrian statue of Louis XIV in the centre of the square — Sun King on a caracoling horse, dressed as a Roman emperor, but still in his wig

inline_foreign_phrases.gloss: marshal

source_passage: Ahead is the Place des Victoires, more famous today for its designer shops than for the victories of the Sun King it commemorates. François d'Aubusson, Maréchal and Duc de La Feuillade, idolized his King and decided to put up a statue in his honour on his own property and at his own expense. The statue was all covered with gold and adorned with His Majesty's court cloak. Its head was disproportionately large, overpowering the rest of the body and decorated with a laurel wreath. On the pedestal, at his feet, four chained women embodied dramatically the King's trampled enemies — Spain, Holland, Germany and Franche-Comté. [...] he called upon the genius of Jules Hardouin-Mansart. The result was the elegant Place des Victoires [...]. La Feuillade, by then the laughing stock of Paris, is said to have relieved the King when he finally gave up the ghost! The statue was naturally melted down during the Revolution, but was replaced by another one during the Restoration. This time the sculptor Bosio seated the Sun King on a caracoling horse, dressed him up as a Roman emperor, but kept his wig!

script_body: When Richelieu built this palace, it was known as le Palais-Cardinal. He bequeathed it to Louis XIII, and after the king's death the royal family moved in. It sat conveniently close to Mazarin's home on neighbouring rue Neuve-des-Petits-Champs, so a door was fitted into the wall around the palace to facilitate his rendezvous with Anne of Austria. That door proved handy in 1650 during the princely revolt of the Fronde, when the Queen and her two sons — the future Louis XIV and Philippe d'Orléans — escaped to Saint-Germain-en-Laye through it.

source_passage: When the palace was built for Richelieu it was known as le Palais-Cardinal. Richelieu bequeathed it to Louis XIII and after the latter's death the royal family moved in. It was conveniently situated close to Mazarin's home on the neighbouring rue Neuve-des-Petits-Champs. To facilitate his rendezvous with Anne of Austria, a door was fitted into the wall that surrounded the palace. It proved handy in 1650, during the princely revolt of the Fronde, when the Queen and her two sons, the future Louis XIV and Philippe d'Orléans, escaped to Saint-Germain-en-Laye.

script_body: The fifth Duc d'Orléans — Philippe, father of the future King Louis-Philippe — was in deep debt when he took over the Palais-Royal. He built the arcades and their shops, rented them out, turned the establishment into a profitable business. Gambling houses and brothels opened up too. His new line was not to the taste of his royal cousin: "Cousin," said Louis XVI disdainfully, "you have turned shop-keeper and no doubt we shall see you only on Sundays." Philippe had his revenge. In 1793 he joined the Revolution, sat in the Convention as "Philippe Égalité," and voted for the death of the king. The guillotine took charge of him too, only a few months later.

physical_cues.cue: Arcades and shops of the Palais-Royal, built by the fifth Duc d'Orléans to pay off his debts

source_passage: His grandson Philippe, the Fifth Duc d'Orléans and father of the future King Louis-Philippe, was in deep debt when he took over the Palais-Royal. He therefore built the arcades and their shops which he rented out, turning the establishment into a profitable business. Gambling houses and brothels opened up too [...]. The Duke's new line of activities was not to the taste of Louis XVI: "Cousin," he said disdainfully, "you have turned shop-keeper and no doubt we shall see you only on Sundays." Philippe d'Orléans would have his revenge: in 1793, having sided with the Revolution, he became member of the Convention under the name of Philippe Égalité and voted for the death of his royal cousin [...]. The guillotine, however, took charge of him too, only a few months later.
