script_body: Near the front of the square a statue of Saint-Denis holds his severed head, overlooking the fountain and mall shaded by plane trees. According to legend, when Denis, the first bishop of Lutetia, was decapitated by the Romans, c. 258 AD — the site traditionally believed to be at the foot of the butte in rue Yvonne le Tac just east of Place des Abbesses — he carried his bloody head up to the spring that until the nineteenth century flowed here, washed it, and then continued north to the site of the Basilica of Saint-Denis, where he is buried. The origin of the name 'Montmartre' is commonly thought to be Mons Martyrum, after the story of the martyrdom of Denis and his two companions.

script_body: The square is named for a victim of a modern totalitarian regime, Suzanne Levy Buisson, born in 1883. At the rue Girardin entrance, a 'Histoire de Paris' plaque identifies her as a martyr of the Resistance and secretary of the Women's Socialist Party. Arrested and tortured by the Nazis, she revealed nothing about the movement. Deported, she died in Germany, the date of her death not known. So little is known about Suzanne Buisson and the other Résistantes that her story and the near anonymity of the plaque's profile inject a dissonance into this hilltop place so filled with light.

script_body: Standing at the entrance of the square, the author invokes Maurice Ravel, who knew Montmartre. In the face of a personal disaster, Ravel once said: 'I firmly believe that joy is far more fertile than pain.' In this Montmartre homage to the memory of Suzanne Buisson and Saint-Denis — in this pretty corner of Paris — there is in their courage a distinct vibration of joy.

A scene from Jean-Pierre Melville's Montmartre film Bob le flambeur takes place here, with the armless woman distinct in the background as Bob the compassionate crook talks business with a partner on a park bench.

script_body: There is graffiti on a wall: 'Le peuple n'obtient que ce qu'il prend' — 'The people only get what they take.' Montmartre was from the first a neighborhood of workers, artisans, and the poor. It's mythologised now as a paradise of the well-heeled and successful artist — Picasso and company — but parts of it were always the territory of rebels, outsiders, and students who couldn't afford the rents in other parts of Paris.

script_body: Square Léon-Serpollet is a people's garden built on terraces, on the former sites of artists' ateliers. The square opens onto the terraces through a pretty arbor and spreads out as you ascend, next to an elementary school. In nearby Place Pecqueur, a sculpted relief of an emigration scene by Steinlein stands watch.

script_body: The approach to rue Cortot from the metro is an exhilarating and scenic climb up the Montmartre hill (butte): follow rue des Abbesses west, right to rue Tholoze, then right again into curvy rue Lepic — the old quarry road where Vincent Van Gogh lived with his brother Theo at number 54 in 1886–1888 and where the only windmills of Montmartre still stand — continue uphill along rue Norvins until the left downhill turn into rue des Saules of the willow trees, and, finally, right into the picturesque rue Cortot. The entrance to the garden is through the bookshop of the Musée de Montmartre.

script_body: The loveliness of the garden's setting is matched by the museum itself — a seventeenth-century house first owned by an actor-colleague of Molière's. In spring its borders are thick with tulips, a softening grace under tall old trees. Beyond the lily pond and the rear garden are views of the small backyard gardens of rue Cortot and, below them, the Montmartre vineyards, parallel to rue des Saules — all of it feels like a generous reward for the rigors of the ascent, knowing you've escaped the crowds thronging Place du Tertre and the steps of Sacré-Coeur.

script_body: In the Middle Ages, the abbesses of Montmartre owned huge estates up here. Henri IV occupied the original twelfth-century Benedictine Abbey — founded by Louis the Fat — during the Siege of Paris in 1589. His artillery dug in on the top of Montmartre as he bombarded the starving city below, which was defended from the Protestant Henri by armed monks and priests. 'My mistress — Paris — is very cruel to me,' he complained. Having neither wife nor mistress on hand, he seduced the Abbess Claude and another nun in his convent headquarters, rewarding them later with control of the abbeys of Vernon and Montmartre. Today the tiny restored church of Saint-Pierre de Montmartre, behind Sacré-Coeur, is the last surviving vestige of the great abbey where Henri IV flirted with the Catholic Church.

script_body: The museum also has a few remnants of 'Red Montmartre,' where the Paris Commune began in 1871. There's a bust of the Communards' emblematic heroine, Louise Michel (1830–1905), the schoolteacher who inspired the seventy-day resistance to the government's army and fought to claim the city for the people who had nothing. She read Baudelaire in the trenches, directed the construction and defense of the barricades, and led more than ten thousand women to fight with her during the bloody and brutal week — la semaine sanglante — of May 1871. Many artists and intellectuals supported the rebels or participated themselves in the civil war, including Courbet, Pissarro, Rimbaud, and Verlaine.

script_body: Renoir lived in this house and knew the nearby moulins — used as dance halls by workers on weekends — painting the famous Bal du Moulin de la Galette in 1876 (now in the Musée d'Orsay). Raoul Dufy had his studio in the right wing in 1901. In Van Gogh's time, the hill was dotted with twenty-five windmills — moulins — which were being converted into dance halls and cabarets, a feature at the heart of Montmartre's reputation as a neighborhood of pleasure and adventure.

script_body: Van Gogh saw desolation beneath the gaiety of Montmartre — a perception shared by his literary contemporaries, poets Paul Verlaine and Arthur Rimbaud and novelist Emile Zola. What did inspire Van Gogh was the panoramic prospect from the butte: the vast city below, often shrouded in fog and smoke, and the Seine running through it. The impressionists, in particular, were inspired by the rural atmosphere and the wide sky over the highest point in Paris.

script_body: Parc Turlure sits north of Sacré-Coeur, where you hear nothing of the hordes and buses in front of it. The most scenic approach is along the village-like rue Saint-Vincent, past Au Lapin Agile — a cabaret-bar favored by Picasso, Modigliani, and Utrillo — uphill, past the beautiful intersection with rue Mont-Cenis framed by tall, elegant, ivy-covered mansions with a long view across northern canyons of steep steps, until you wind right into rue de la Bonne and the entrance to the park. With your back to the cascading artificial waterfall and Sacré-Coeur, you look out over the high brick mansions of Montmartre on the slopes below. Inside the shade of the arbor court, thick with greenery, there is silence and the fragrance of jasmine, which is everywhere.

script_body: My Parisian friends prefer New York City's High Line to their own Coulee Verte, the first of the abandoned railroad viaducts transformed in the 1990s into a landscaped walkway above the streets of a big city. The newer High Line is wider than the Promenade Plantee, more open to the wind off the Hudson River, the plantings more diverse. Walking the Promenade from Bastille to the Jardin de Reuilly — a midway point — you have a sense of enclosure, of feeling protected along this lush corridor of flowering cherry trees, spirea, jasmine, quince. A still place, except for the play of shadows and sunlight or the slow movement of walkers, the Promenade provides plenty of benches for taking a break and enjoying the views: the small rooftop gardens of the apartments to the north that face the walkway, and the architectural facades to the south. Like a secular outdoor cloister walk that goes somewhere — as far as the Bois de Vincennes if you stay the three-mile course — the Promenade in early evening has a meditative calm.

script_body: There's something thrilling about this overview of the streets of northeastern Paris, the home ground of les classes dangereuses — the dangerous classes. So much tumultuous history erupted in these quartiers below the old railroad tracks, part of the Paris-Cherbourg line. The political uproars and retreats of the arrondissements of northeastern Paris come closer to the actual character of the city — its multiple faces and voices — than the tamed tourist areas to the west. Looking down, you can imagine your own scenarios, the atrocities of poverty and injustice that once made these streets the cradle of revolution.

Walter Benjamin noted the effect of glass on the city around it: 'Paris is a city of mirrors. The asphalt of its roadways smooth as glass, and at the entrance to all bistros glass partitions. A profusion of windowpanes and mirrors in cafes, so as to make the inside brighter and to give all the tiny nooks and crannies, into which Parisian taverns separate, a pleasing amplitude.'

script_body: The Bois de Vincennes began, like the Bois de Boulogne to the west, as a royal hunting ground in the twelfth century. The thirteenth-century King — later Saint — Louis IX, as first judge of the realm, famously met his subjects and heard their cases under an oak tree in the Vincennes forest: 'Seated on a scarlet blanket, dressed in a simple coat of wool but with a cap of peacock feathers, [he] delivered decisions without concern for wealth or social rank.' The saintly Louis, canonized in 1297, walked back and forth between Vincennes and Paris, building a chapel in both places.

Hundreds of species flourish here: a garden of orchids from early March, a dahlia garden in fall, a garden of water lilies and lotus, a forest of camellias, a vast wavelike display of tulips from April on, fields of irises, azaleas, and rhododendrons in May. As you walk the long and dusty courtyard of the military grounds today, you notice there is nothing growing anywhere, not one blade of grass.

script_body: Square Maurice-Gardette stands on former abattoir grounds where history left its deepest stain. In the surrounding streets — rue Saint-Maur, avenue Parmentier — Communards defended their barricades in 1871, and were eventually slaughtered. Piles of corpses filled these streets. During the German Occupation, the Gestapo and gendarmes were a brutal force in this quartier. The square today sits in the eleventh arrondissement, historically the poorest, most populated, and most insurrectionary area of Paris — a neighborhood that has absorbed more violence than most cities see in a generation.

script_body: The square is named for Maurice Gardette (1895–1941), a metalworker born and raised in poverty who lived with his wife and children in nearby rue Chemin Vert. A member of the French Communist Party elected to the city council, he was arrested for his antifascist activism. On October 22, 1941, he wrote on a plank in the barracks of a prison camp: "Je meurs courageux, plein de foi révolutionnaire" — "I die courageously, full of revolutionary faith." He and twenty-six comrades of the Resistance were shot at Châteaubriant that same day. On October 20, 2010, the mairie of the eleventh commemorated the sixty-ninth anniversary of his death. Local people and politicians gathered in the square, a few elderly Resistants among them, sang songs from World War II, then marched to Père-Lachaise, where the bodies and ashes of Gardette and the other Fusillés de Châteaubriant — including Jean-Pierre Timbaud and seventeen-year-old Guy Moquet — are buried, across from the Mur des Fédérés.

A member of the French Communist Party, elected to the city council, he was arrested for his antifascist activism. On October 22, 1941, he wrote on a plank in the barracks of the prison camp: "Je meurs courageux, plein de foi revolutionnaire"—"I die courageously, full of revolutionary faith." The citizens of 2010—among them a few elderly Resistants—listened to speeches, sang songs popular during World War II, then marched to Pere-Lachaise, where the bodies and ashes of Maurice Gardette and the other Fusilles de Chateaubriant (including Jean-Pierre Timbaud and seventeen-year-old Guy Moquet) are buried, across from the Mur des Federes.

Placed within this thick, colorful greenery is a bronze sculpture by Jacques Perrin: Le Botteleur, an arresting representation of a worker bending over in a field to tie the work of his hands into bunches.

script_body: Today, the square's memory is shaped not by its violent past but by the Resistance and survival of that force. Historian Alan Riding notes that during the war years following Maurice Gardette's murder, 75 percent of French Jews were saved from deportation and death — despite the longtime anti-Semitism of the French right wing — "owing to the courage of countless French men and women — teachers, priests, nuns, resistance fighters, doctors, farmers, and others." As Milan Kundera wrote, "The struggle against power is the struggle of memory against forgetting." This annual fall ritual of patriotic observance keeps the historical memory of the eleventh alive.

The memory honored in Square Maurice-Gardette in October 2010 fertilizes the green heart of Paris, saves it from historical amnesia. (As Milan Kundera has said, "The struggle against power is the struggle of memory against forgetting.")

script_body: At the square's entrance, a "History of Paris" plaque at the windows of the still-standing guardhouse tells a grim story. After the convent of nuns here was closed following 1789, Roquette became for centuries a site of incarceration: of women, of incorrigible children ages six to twenty, and finally of four thousand Resistantes during the German Occupation. The men's prison for murderers and death-row inmates stood across rue de la Roquette in rue de la Croix Faubin, where the guillotine — "that shameful machine of human butchery," in the words of Louise Michel — operated until it was demolished in 1974. The square now occupies the footprint of this architecture of tyranny, its prisons that once "looked like towering grim castles."

script_body: Square de la Roquette is built on a kind of butte, its winding paths bench-lined and skirting flower beds that are glorious in spring: hyacinth, pansies, daisies, snowdrops, wildflowers, tulips all bloom beneath magnolias, palm trees, and eucalyptus. Just inside the entrance, a high cascading fountain waters the palm trees and flower gardens. Local people — there are few strangers here — sit in the companionable shade. Like so many calm green sanctuaries in Paris, this landscape bears a legacy of pain from the old world, but has been made over in the image of a more generous polity, an urban oasis replacing an architecture of tyranny.

script_body: Since the revolution of 1968 — euphemistically referred to as les événements, or "the events" of 1968 — this old area of insurrection, the plebeian northeast of the eleventh, twelfth, nineteenth, and twentieth arrondissements, has been reconstituted. After years of demolition and gentrification under former president Georges Pompidou (1969–1974), the mixed population returned. In the streets around rue de la Roquette, the Paris proletariat reestablished itself, marked by the return of immigrants, working families, artists, and "an intellectual but nonuniversity youth."

After years of demolition and gentrification under former president Georges Pompidou (1969—1974), the mixed population has returned. In the streets around rue de la Roquette, the Paris proletariat has reestablished itself, marked by the return of immigrants, working families, artists, and "an intellectual but nonuniversity youth."

script_body: Walking from central or western Paris into the northeast enables what one theorist calls "psychogeography" — "the sudden change of ambience in a street within the space of a few meters, the evident division of the city into zones of distinct psychic atmospheres." Walkers are, in this view, "practitioners of the city": "the city is a language . . . and walking is the act of speaking that language." Only by using one's legs to move from one arrondissement to another does it become obvious: the City of Light speaks many languages.

Only by using one's leg power to see one arrondissement after another can you get inside that language. Moving on foot from central or western Paris into the northeast enables the physical and emotional reverberations of "psychogeography," the sense of "the sudden change of ambience in a street within the space of a few meters, the evident division of the city into zones of distinct psychic atmospheres."

fact_check.notes: The 'psychogeography' concept is attributed to the Situationist International (Guy Debord). The walking quote is attributed in the book's footnote to Rebecca Solnit, 'Paris, or Botanizing on the Asphalt,' in Wanderlust: A History of Walking.

script_body: Beneath the pleasant lawns of Buttes-Chaumont lies a history of medieval horror. In the Middle Ages, as far to the west as Place du Colonel-Fabien, this land was the site of the gibbet of Montfaucon — established by Saint Louis (1223–70) as a sign of royal justice over the city. It was an elaborate stone structure with some 16 columns, each ten meters high. From it literally scores of decaying criminals' bodies could be hanging at any time. The gibbet was a place of execution in its own right, but also the place of exhibition of the remains of individuals tortured and executed in one of the many execution sites in Paris. Bodies could be left there for two or three years or more, at the end of which time, crows and — in bad times — wolves having done their worst — they were a gruesome sight, and their noisome stench wafted towards the Faubourg du Temple. In its garbage dump years, this landscape also fed a plump army of rats, who could strip a corpse to its skeleton within 24 hours.

script_body: Monsieur Alphand had his work cut out for him when Haussmann and Napoleon III directed him to transform the foul terrain in eastern Paris into a scenic garden that would become Buttes-Chaumont. Some visitors are aware that in an earlier life the park served as a quarry for gypsum — plaster of Paris — as well as a garbage dump. But the genius landscape engineer and architect pulled off an inspired metamorphosis: today Buttes-Chaumont is one of the city's most popular parks, where sprawling and picnicking on the grass is permitted to weekending crowds from all over the city.

script_body: The robust and exuberant Julia Child, early in her time as a Parisian, found her way to Buttes-Chaumont on foot with her husband Paul: "Paris was wonderfully walkable. . . . one could easily hike from the Place de la Concorde to the top of Montmartre in a half-hour. . . . One cold afternoon just before New Year's, Paul and I strolled up to the Buttes-Chaumont park. At the top of the hill, by the little Greek temple, we looked back at Sacré-Coeur on Montmartre, now silhouetted through layers of mist by the declining sun." Then they retired to a nearby cozy bistro, complete with cats, dogs, neighborhood characters, and two monkeys squealing and chattering.

source_passage: Many tourists do not make it out this far from the city center, but the robust and exuberant Julia Child (with her husband, Paul) found her way, on foot, early in her time as a Parisian: Paris was wonderfully walkable. . . . one could easily hike from the Place de la Concorde to the top of Montmartre in a half-hour. . . . At the top of the hill, by the little Greek temple, we looked back at Sacre-Coeur on Montmartre, now silhouetted through layers of mist by the declining sun. ... Then they retired to a nearby cozy bistro, complete with cats, dogs, neighborhood characters, and two monkeys squealing and chattering.

The park goes on and on for miles, past one innovative themed garden after another — the Garden of Mirrors, of Dunes, of Winds, of Shadows, of Dragons (with a dragon slide) — all joined together by the Promenade des Jardins. Other highlights near the southern entrance include the Conservatoire de Paris, the Musée de la Musique with five floors of instruments, and the Cité de la Musique auditorium.

script_body: Colette (1873–1954), ecstatic lover of nature, would approve mightily of her final resting place. There are twelve thousand trees in Père-Lachaise Cemetery, avenues of cypresses, sycamores, tall, ancient chestnuts, a thick sheltering green roof over the cemetery's 105 acres of unspoiled beauty. Flowers are planted around the graves, some garlanding the monuments, symbolizing perpetual affection for the dead. "Throughout my existence," Colette wrote not long before she died, "I have studied flowering more than any other manifestation of life. It is there, for me, that the essential drama resides, and not in death, which is just a banal defeat."

script_body: Among the 300,000 men and women buried in Paris's largest cemetery are icons of a prodigious flowering of French civilization — writers, painters, sculptors, singers, composers, and cineastes who make us love life more. You can stroll the silent hillsides, follow the long winding cobbled paths, stirred to your depths as you suddenly come upon the graves of Proust and Wilde, Delescluze, Daumier, and Poulenc. Memory, said Gertrude Stein: the only true immortality. Her grave is at the eastern edge of avenue Circulaire.

Time spent in Pere-Lachaise quickens that love. There's no hurry here, no distractions. You can stroll the silent hillsides, follow the long, winding cobbled paths, stirred to your depths as you suddenly come upon the graves of Proust and Wilde, Delescluze, Daumier, and Poulenc. You can stop midway at a bench along a steep avenue to contemplate this landscape of memory. Memory, said Gertrude Stein: the only true immortality. script_body: From the heights of Père-Lachaise you can trace a remarkable cluster of nineteenth-century genius on your map. Chopin lies down the hill near the center, not far from Colette, or from another of George Sand's lovers, Alfred de Musset. Delacroix, buried under black lava to the west, was the romantic painter's version of his beloved Chopin's romantic music — his artistic style a striving for a surprising violent exotic beauty. Balzac, another friend of Delacroix and another genius of that great nineteenth-century artistic explosion, rests in the same section.

script_body: In the vicinity of Colette's flower-strewn black granite grave are the lovers Héloïse (1101–1164) and Abélard (1079–1142), together in death in eternal defiance of the ecclesiastical powers that forced them apart in life. Their bodies were moved into Père-Lachaise — along with Molière and La Fontaine — in an effort to attract the important dead to what was a remote section of Paris when the cemetery was opened by Napoleon in 1804.

script_body: In the seventeenth century the land of what is now Père-Lachaise had belonged to the Jesuits, who called it Mont Louis. The prominent Jesuit Francis de la Chaise d'Aix, confessor to Louis XIV, lived here and retired to a splendid country house on Mont Louis. Supposedly, the simpatico confessor and the young king-to-be watched the civil revolt called the Fronde (1649–1652) from here — "the hill of Charonne" — that traumatic vigil the source of the Sun King's lifelong fear and hatred of the mob, the frondeurs, which would eventually drive him to abandon Paris and move the royal court to Versailles.

script_body: Two hundred years after Louis XIV's Fronde vigil, the Paris Communards made their last stand here among the tombstones — and in the nearby streets of Ménilmontant, Charonne, and Belleville. Finally subdued on May 28, 1871, 147 rebels were rounded up and shot against the eastern perimeter wall; the corpses of another thousand Communards were dumped in pits against the same wall. Today the Mur des Fédérés — the Wall of the Communards — to the right and down a few steps off avenue Circulaire — is a site of annual pilgrimage to commemorate the bravery of the working classes and the savagery of a government terrified of popular revolt. Now classified as a national historical monument, the Wall is always decorated with the flowers and wreaths left by pilgrims who arrive in all seasons.

script_body: Saint-Sulpice is the second-largest church in Paris, dedicated to Sulpitius the Pious. The present building — the second on the site, raised over a Romanesque church from the 13th century — was founded in 1646 by the parish priest Jean-Jacques Olier, who had established the Society of Saint-Sulpice, a clerical congregation, and a seminary attached to the church. Anne of Austria laid the first stone.

script_body: At the far end of the church, in the Lady Chapel, stands a large white marble statue of the Virgin by Jean-Baptiste Pigalle. It is a replacement. The original was solid silver, sculpted by Edmé Bouchardon and cast from silverware donated by the parishioners — and it was known as "Our Lady of the Old Tableware." That silver Virgin vanished at the time of the Revolution, and Pigalle's marble figure, ringed by stucco from Louis-Philippe Mouchy, has stood in her place ever since.

script_body: When the architect Gilles-Marie Oppenord was working on the transept in the 1720s, he built a bell tower on top of the crossing, around 1725. It was a costly miscalculation: the tower's own weight threatened to collapse the structure, and it had to be removed. This may account for what came next — Oppenord was relieved of his duties as an architect and restricted to designing decoration.

script_body: The pulpit in the nave, designed by Charles de Wailly and completed in 1788, has a quirk: its oak canopy broadcasts sound so well it needs no amplification. It also became a stage for revolution. From here the parish priest of Saint-Sulpice declared his refusal to accept the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, and revolutionary orators used it later too. During the Paris Commune of 1871, the church served as headquarters of a faction called the Club de la Victoire, and Louise Michel spoke from this same pulpit.

script_body: When Dan Brown's 2003 novel The Da Vinci Code became an international bestseller, it brought crowds of tourists to Saint-Sulpice hunting for the secrets the book claimed were hidden here. The church pushed back with a note on display for visitors: the brass line in the floor is not the vestige of a pagan temple, it was never called a "Rose-Line," and the letters P and S in the round transept windows stand for Peter and Sulpice, the church's patron saints — not for any imaginary "Priory of Sion." In 2005, the Archdiocese of Paris refused Ron Howard permission to film inside the church for the movie.

script_body: You're standing at the smaller of Paris's two triumphal arches. Napoleon had it raised between 1806 and 1808 to commemorate his victories in the Wars of the Third and Fourth Coalitions, in the Neoclassical style, its columns set in the Corinthian order. Look down the long axis to the west and you can pick out its far more famous sibling, the Arc de Triomphe de l'Étoile, at the end of the Champs-Élysées — about twice this size. The two were designed in the same year, though that larger arch wasn't completed until 1836.

physical_cues.cue: the view west down the long axis toward the distant Arc de Triomphe de l'Étoile

key_claims: Neoclassical arch in the Corinthian order, built 1806-1808 for Napoleon's victories in the Wars of the Third and Fourth Coalitions
The Arc de Triomphe de l'Étoile at the end of the Champs-Élysées is about twice the size, designed the same year but finished only in 1836
source_passage: It is an example of Neoclassical architecture in the Corinthian order. It was built between 1806 and 1808 to commemorate Napoleon's military victories in the Wars of the Third and Fourth Coalitions. The Arc de Triomphe de l'Étoile, at the far end of the Champs-Élysées, is about twice the size; designed in the same year but not completed until 1836.

script_body: The arch was designed by Charles Percier and Pierre François Léonard Fontaine and raised for the Emperor Napoleon the First between 1806 and 1808. They modelled it openly on ancient Rome — in particular the Arch of Septimius Severus, and the Arch of Constantine, built there in the year 312. Around the outside stand eight Corinthian columns of marble. Those columns weren't cut for the arch at all: they were salvaged from the Château de Meudon, which had been pulled down in 1804.

physical_cues.cue: the eight marble Corinthian columns around the arch's exterior

key_claims: Designed by Charles Percier and Pierre François Léonard Fontaine, built 1806-1808 for Napoleon I
Modelled on Roman arches — the Arch of Septimius Severus and the Arch of Constantine (312 AD)
Its eight Corinthian marble columns were recovered from the Château de Meudon, destroyed in 1804
source_passage: Designed by Charles Percier and Pierre François Léonard Fontaine, the arch was built between 1806 and 1808 by the Emperor Napoleon I, on the model of the Arch of Constantine (312 AD) in Rome, as a gateway of the Tuileries Palace, the Imperial residence. Around its exterior are eight Corinthian columns of marble. These columns were recovered from the Château de Meudon, destroyed in 1804. The arch is derivative of the triumphal arches of the Roman Empire, in particular the Arch of Septimius Severus in Rome.

script_body: The carved panels set into the arch are a roll-call of Napoleon's triumphs, worked in rose-coloured marble. Among them are the Battle of Austerlitz, the surrender of Ulm, the entrances into Vienna and Munich, the Peace of Pressburg, and the conference at Tilsit. The battle subjects were chosen by Vivant Denon, director of the Musée Napoléon — then housed in the Louvre — and drawn up by Charles Meynier.

script_body: Look up to the tops of the columns. Each is crowned by a marble soldier, and together the eight figures reproduce, in careful detail, the uniforms of the principal corps of Napoleon's imperial army. Only one of them portrays a real man. The sapper is modelled on Dominique Gaye Mariolle, a soldier known for his strength and for a height that topped two metres. He is remembered for a single gesture: during a review of the troops before Tilsit, in July 1807, he presented a cannon to Napoleon in place of a rifle.

He famously presented a cannon instead of a rifle at Napoleon's troop review before Tilsit, July 1807

He is famous for having presented a cannon instead of a rifle during Napoleon's review of his troops prior to the battle of Tilsitt in July 1807.

script_body: The chariot and horses on top of the arch carry a story of conquest and reversal. When the arch went up, it was crowned by the Horses of Saint Mark, taken from St Mark's Basilica in Venice — Napoleon had seized them in 1798. They didn't stay long. In 1815, after the defeat at Waterloo and the return of the Bourbon kings, France ceded the horses to the Austrian Empire, which then held Venice under the Congress of Vienna; the Austrians sent them straight back to Venice. So in 1828 they were replaced by the group you see now, sculpted by Baron François Joseph Bosio: Peace riding in a triumphal chariot, led by gilded Victories on either side — raised not to Napoleon, but to the restored Bourbon monarchy that had outlasted him.

physical_cues.cue: the quadriga of Peace in a chariot, led by gilded Victories, atop the arch

key_claims: Originally crowned by the Horses of Saint Mark, seized from Venice by Napoleon in 1798
Returned to Venice in 1815 after Waterloo via the Austrian Empire and the Congress of Vienna
Replaced in 1828 by Bosio's quadriga of Peace led by gilded Victories, commemorating the Bourbon Restoration
source_passage: It was originally surmounted by the Horses of Saint Mark from St Mark's Basilica in Venice, which had been captured in 1798 by Napoleon. In 1815, following the Battle of Waterloo and the Bourbon restoration, France ceded the quadriga to the Austrian Empire which had annexed Venice under the terms of the Congress of Vienna. The Austrians immediately returned the statuary to Venice. The horses of Saint Mark were replaced in 1828 by a quadriga sculpted by Baron François Joseph Bosio, depicting Peace riding in a triumphal chariot led by gilded Victories on both sides. The composition commemorates the Restoration of the Bourbons following Napoleon's downfall.

script_body: This arch was never meant to stand on its own. It was built as the ceremonial gateway to the Tuileries Palace, the imperial residence that once closed off this end of the Louvre. That palace is gone — destroyed in 1871, during the Paris Commune — and clearing its ruins opened the long, unobstructed view west, straight toward the distant Arc de Triomphe. What you're standing on is the eastern end of the Axe historique, the 'historic axis': a roughly nine-kilometre line running out across the northwestern quarter of the city, arch aligned with arch all the way to the horizon.

physical_cues.cue: the open western view down the axis toward the distant Arc de Triomphe, where the Tuileries Palace once stood

key_claims: Built as the ceremonial gateway to the Tuileries Palace, the imperial residence
The palace was destroyed in the 1871 Paris Commune, opening the unobstructed western view
The arch marks the eastern end of the nine-kilometre Axe historique
source_passage: as a gateway of the Tuileries Palace, the Imperial residence. The destruction of the Tuileries Palace during the Paris Commune in 1871, allowed an unobstructed view west towards the Arc de Triomphe. The Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel is at the eastern end of Paris Axe historique ("historic axis"), a nine-kilometre-long linear route which dominates much of the northwestern quadrant of the city.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; the arch stands on the historic axis and all described features (quadriga, soldier statues, marble columns, bas-reliefs) remain in place.

script_body: Galeries Lafayette began in 1894, when Théophile Bader and his cousin Alphonse Kahn opened a fashion store in a small haberdasher's shop at the corner of rue La Fayette and the Chaussée d'Antin. The little haberdashery grew fast: in 1896 the company bought the entire building at 1 rue La Fayette, and in 1905 it acquired the buildings at 38, 40 and 42 boulevard Haussmann, along with 15 rue de la Chaussée d'Antin — the footprint of the flagship store that fills this corner today.

physical_cues.cue: The flagship store's frontage along 38–42 boulevard Haussmann

source_passage: In 1894, Théophile Bader and his cousin Alphonse Kahn opened a fashion store in a small haberdasher's shop at the corner of rue La Fayette and the Chaussée d'Antin, in Paris. In 1896, their company purchased the entire building at 1 rue La Fayette; in 1905 they acquired the buildings at 38, 40 and 42 boulevard Haussmann and 15 rue de la Chaussée d'Antin.

script_body: Look up: the dome that crowns the store rises forty-three metres overhead, a Neo-Byzantine canopy of glass and steel. It was designed by Ferdinand Chanut, the apprentice of the architect Georges Chedanne — Chedanne had led the store's first major renovations, completed in 1907. The dome and the building's Art Nouveau staircases were finished in 1912, and the store was inaugurated that October. Two decades later, in 1932, the interior was reworked in Art Déco style by the architect Pierre Patou.

physical_cues.cue: The forty-three-metre glass-and-steel dome overhead
The store's Art Nouveau staircases

source_passage: Bader commissioned the architect Georges Chedanne and his pupil Ferdinand Chanut to design the store at the Haussmann location, where a glass and steel dome and Art Nouveau staircases were finished in 1912. Théophile Bader appointed the architect Georges Chedanne to head up the first major renovations which were completed in 1907. Ferdinand Chanut, Georges Chedanne's apprentice, designed the store's 43-metre (141 ft) high Neo Byzantine dome. This store's inauguration ceremony took place in October 1912. In 1932, the store was renovated with an Art Déco style by architect Pierre Patou.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; dome remains the store's iconic feature

script_body: During the Nazi occupation of France, Galeries Lafayette was stripped from its Jewish owners. In 1940 the store underwent a process of 'Aryanization' — the forced removal of those owners and their replacement by non-Jewish ones. Théophile Bader, Raoul Meyer, Max Heilbronn, the store's administrators and 129 Jewish employees were all made to resign. The property of the Bader, Meyer and Heilbronn families was taken, and the company itself was transferred to new owners: the Swiss Aubert and the French industrialist Harlachol.
source_passage: During Nazi occupation of France in 1940, Les Galeries Lafayette underwent a process of "Aryanization", that is the removal of Jewish owners and their replacement by non-Jewish owners. Théophile Bader, Raoul Meyer, Max Heilbronn, the store's administrators and 129 Jewish employees were forced to resign. The property of Bader, Meyer and Heilbronn families was taken. The Galeries Lafayette group was transferred to non-Jewish owners: the Swiss Aubert and the French industrialist Harlachol.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions

In 1984 the store opened a dedicated designer department carrying the work of Jean-Paul Gaultier and Thierry Mugler.

script_body: Like the other great Paris department stores, Galeries Lafayette ran its own decorative-arts atelier. Called the Maîtrise workshop and directed from 1921 by Maurice Dufrêne, it produced affordable furniture, fabric, carpets, wallpaper, pottery and other household goods. It was one of several such in-house design studios: Printemps had its Primavera, Le Bon Marché its Pomone under Paul Follot, and the Grands Magasins du Louvre its Studium.
source_passage: From 1921 Maurice Dufrêne directed the Maîtrise workshop of the Galeries Lafayette. This workshop for decorative art and furniture followed the Primavera of the Printemps store founded in 1912 by René Guilleré, Paul Follot's Pomone of Le Bon Marché, and the Studium of the Grands Magasins du Louvre. In 1922, it opened arts workshops under the artistic direction of Maurice Dufrêne in order to produce affordable furniture, fabric, carpets, wallpaper, pottery, and other household goods.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; La Maitrise (Dufrene) and rival ateliers Primavera/Pomone/Studium are well documented Art Deco history

script_body: This site holds a survivor far older than the exchange itself. Between 1574 and 1584, the architect Jean Bullant built a grand hôtel particulier here for Catherine de' Medici, and beside it rose a tower with an encaged observation platform — now known as the Medici column — from which the stars could be observed for astrological purposes. The queen's house later passed to the Count of Soissons, becoming the Hôtel de Soissons; but its last owner died in debt, and in 1748 the house was demolished and its materials sold to pay the creditors. The column alone was spared: that same year, the writer Louis Petit de Bachaumont bought it and saved it from destruction.

physical_cues.cue: The Medici column standing on the site

source_passage: Between 1574 and 1584 Jean Bullant (1515–78) built a hôtel particulier (grand house) on the site for Catherine de' Medici (1519–89). A tower with an encaged observation platform, now called the Medici column, was built beside the hôtel from which observations of the stars could be made for astrological purposes. The Queen's hôtel was bought by Charles de Bourbon-Condé, Count of Soissons, who repaired and enlarged it. The hotel became called the Hôtel de Soissons. The indebted last owner was Victor Amadeus of Savoy (1690–1741). After his death the hotel was demolished in 1748 and the materials sold to pay the creditors. The city of Paris bought the column from its first owner, Laurent Destouches, which saved it from destruction.

script_body: The round building you stand in began as a granary. Between 1763 and 1767, the City of Paris raised a circular hall here for the storage and sale of wheat — the Halle aux blés, or Wheat Exchange, designed by Nicolas Le Camus de Mézières around a circular central courtyard reached by a double staircase. That eighteenth-century layout has been kept ever since; the ring you walk today still traces the old grain market's plan.

source_passage: Between 1763 and 1767 the City of Paris built a circular building on the site for the storage and sale of wheat. The Halle aux blés (Wheat Exchange) was designed by Nicolas Le Camus de Mézières with a circular central courtyard and a double staircase. The layout of that building has been retained.

script_body: Look up at the dome — the building's crowning glory and today a listed historical monument. The first version, a wooden cupola, was built in 1782–83 by Jacques-Guillaume Legrand and Jacques Molinos, following the principles defined by Philibert de l'Orme. On 16 October 1802 fire destroyed it. After some controversy, a new design by François-Joseph Bélanger was chosen: an iron dome sheathed in copper. Victor Hugo, writing in his 1831 novel Notre-Dame de Paris, described it as 'an English jockey-cap on a large scale.'

physical_cues.cue: The iron-and-copper dome overhead

On 16 October 1802 the cupola was destroyed by fire. A new design by François-Joseph Bélanger for an iron dome covered in sheets of copper was selected after some controversy. Victor Hugo described the dome in his 1831 novel Notre-Dame de Paris as an English jockey-cap on a large scale.

script_body: The building you see owes its present shape to a major reconstruction begun by the architect Henri Blondel in 1885 and carried out in 1888–89. He kept the circular form — twenty-five bays divided by pairs of pilasters — and reworked the structure around the surviving cupola. Above the entrance, look for the pediment: four fluted Corinthian columns carry a sculpted group by Aristide Croisy, in which three allegorical figures represent the City of Paris flanked by Trade and Abundance.

The building designed by Blondel still had a circular shape, with 25 bays separated by two pilasters. Blondel retained but modified the cupola. The entrance portico is surmounted by a pediment supported by four fluted Corinthian columns on which three allegorical figures by the sculptor Aristide Croisy represent the City of Paris flanked by Trade and Abundance.

script_body: In 2016 the mayor of Paris, Anne Hidalgo, offered the collector François Pinault a fifty-year lease on the Bourse de Commerce for a lump sum of fifteen million euros plus yearly fees, and the city approved turning the old exchange into a home for contemporary art. The boldest stroke came from the architect Tadao Ando: a thirty-foot-high concrete cylinder set inside the historic building to serve as the main exhibition gallery, standing within the nineteenth-century shell. Delayed from 2020 by the COVID-19 pandemic, the museum opened in mid-May 2021.

physical_cues.cue: Tadao Ando's concrete cylinder rising inside the rotunda

source_passage: In 2016, the mayor of Paris, Anne Hidalgo, offered François Pinault a 50-year lease on the Bourse de Commerce for a lump sum of €15 million, plus yearly fees. Shortly after, the Paris City Council approved the project to transform the building into an exhibition space for contemporary art, including pieces from Pinault's private collection of more than 3,500 works valued at around €1.25 billion. In 2017, Pinault publicly presented plans by architect Tadao Ando for placing a 30-foot-high concrete cylinder inside the building to be the Bourse's main exhibition gallery, at construction costs of $170 million. The Bourse's initial opening date had been set for summer 2020, before it was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic in France. Instead, it opened in mid-May 2021.

script_body: For more than a century this was a working trading floor. Futures markets ran here from the start — first in wheat, oats, flour, oil, sugar, alcohol and rubber, and after World War II in white sugar, cocoa, coffee, soybean meal and rapeseed. Then, in 1998, computerization ended trading in the building, and the exchange now survives as an electronic market within Euronext.
source_passage: Many futures markets functioned at the Commodities Exchange from its inception, at first under the control of syndicates for wheat, rye and oats, flour, oil, sugar, alcohol, and rubber. After the World War II (1939–45) the futures markets were opened gradually to international trading in goods such as white sugar, cocoa, coffee, potato, soybean meal, and rapeseed. With the computerization of futures markets, in 1998 market activity ended at the Bourse de Commerce building. The exchange continues as an electronic market within Euronext.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; floor trading ended 1998, continues electronically within Euronext

script_body: Step inside and look up at the curved wall beneath the dome. The rotunda is wrapped in a painted panorama, the work of five painters — Alexis-Joseph Mazerolle, Évariste Vital Luminais, Désiré François Laugée, Georges Clairin and Hippolyte Lucas. Painted panels personify the four directions — North, East, South and West — while frescoes depict the history of trade between the five continents. Classified as a historical monument in 1975, the murals were restored in 1998.

Painted panels depict characters that symbolize North, East, South, and West, and frescoes represent the history of trade between the five continents. The murals and cupola were classified as a historical monument on 15 January 1975. The murals were restored in 1998.

script_body: Look at the façade — it is a manifesto of Art Nouveau. Across it run ceramic panels in bright hues of yellow, white, green and gold, and the word 'Samaritaine,' along with some of the wares once sold inside, is spelled out in colourful enamel in elaborate lettering, scattered with naturalistic flower motifs. Two domes of glass brick crown the building and light up at night; their eight-sided verticals draw the eye upward, and together the two domes frame a sight line between the Seine and the left bank. The buildings have been listed as a monument historique by the French Ministry of Culture since 1990.

source_passage: Since 1990 the buildings have been listed as a monument historique by the French Ministry of Culture. The building's exterior has two domes made of glass brick that light up in the nighttime. The extended verticals of the domes, sectioned into eight sides, accentuate the height of the building and draw the viewer's eye to the top of the store. The facade of the building consists of ceramic panels in brightly colored hues of yellow, white, green, and gold. The word "Samaritaine", as well as some of the available merchandise and ware, are displayed around the facade of the building in colorful enamel using an elaborate lettering. Dispersed around these signs are colorful naturalistic flower motifs, which continue to the interior design of the building as well. The two domes of the Samaritaine create a sight line between the Seine and the left bank.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; domes + enamel facade present after restoration; monument historique since 1990

script_body: The Samaritaine you can enter today reopened only recently, after one of Paris's longest store closures. It shut on 15 June 2005, officially to fix urgent fire-safety hazards — though the labour unions suspected a restructuring. LVMH took full ownership in late 2010, but the redevelopment dragged: in January 2015 a French court revoked the building permit and halted the work, and there was opposition to the new façades designed by the Japanese architecture firm SANAA, which the mayor of Paris, Anne Hidalgo, supported. Work resumed, and after sixteen years of closure the store reopened in June 2021 — its doors opened by French President Emmanuel Macron alongside LVMH's CEO Bernard Arnault. The buildings now hold a Cheval Blanc hotel, a nursery, offices and social housing as well.

physical_cues.cue: The new façade designed by SANAA

source_passage: Since 1990 the buildings have been listed as a monument historique by the French Ministry of Culture. The store was closed on 15 June 2005, as the building needed urgent renovations to mitigate fire safety hazards. However labour unions believed it was because of a restructure of the store. LVMH purchased the remaining shares in the department store from the Cognacq-Jay foundation in late 2010, giving LVMH full ownership of the department store. In January 2015 work on the store was halted again after building permission was revoked by a French Court. Work started again despite opposition to the new facades designed by Japanese architecture firm SANAA. The mayor of Paris Anne Hidalgo supported the plans. After sixteen years of closure, the department store was reopened to the public in June 2021, now co-branded as part of DFS. The store was reopened by French President Emmanuel Macron and the CEO of LVMH, Bernard Arnault. The buildings now include a Cheval Blanc hotel, nursery, offices and social housing.

script_body: La Samaritaine takes its name from the river. Ernest Cognacq opened the store in 1870, on the corner of the Rue du Pont-Neuf and the Rue de la Monnaie, and in 1872 he married Marie-Louise Jaÿ, the two of them running it together. The name reached back to an old water pump called the Samaritaine, which until 1813 had stood on the second arch of the nearby Pont Neuf — so the great department store on this corner is named for a vanished pumping station on the bridge beside it. The store is now owned by the luxury goods conglomerate LVMH.

The store was named after the old Samaritaine pumping station, which until 1813 had stood on the second arch of the nearby Pont Neuf.

script_body: The store's architect, Frantz Jourdain, was a leading figure of Art Nouveau — president of the Societe du Nouveau at the movement's height — and he built the Samaritaine in its image. He redesigned the interiors of magasin one — magasin meaning 'store' in French — in 1891, and designed magasin two, which opened in 1910; much of magasin two was pre-fabricated, so it went up quickly. Its skeleton is steel and glass. Then, between 1926 and 1928, Jourdain worked with Henri Sauvage to extend the store toward the river Seine, and by the end of that partnership the Samaritaine had grown into four buildings, eleven floors tall.

The Moulin Rouge opened on 6 October 1889 as the Jardin de Paris, an outdoor garden café-concert at the foot of the Montmartre hill, in the district of Pigalle. It was co-founded by two formidable showmen, Joseph Oller and Charles Zidler, who also owned the Paris Olympia and understood exactly what the public wanted.

script_body: This is the birthplace of the modern can-can. It began here as a seductive dance performed by the courtesans who operated from the site, inspired by the quadrille — an energetic dance done to a lively rhythm in provocative costumes. From the Moulin Rouge the can-can grew into a revue, an entertainment in its own right, and helped spread the cabaret across Europe. Its early stars became legends of the era — la Goulue, Jane Avril, la Môme Fromage, Grille d'Egout, Nini Pattes en l'Air, Valentin le désossé, the singer Yvette Guilbert and the clown Cha-U-Kao.

Originally introduced as a seductive dance by the courtesans who operated from the site, the can-can dance revue evolved into a form of entertainment of its own and led to the introduction of cabarets across Europe. A new dance, inspired by the quadrille and gaining popularity, known as the Can-can. Dancers performed this energetic dance to a lively rhythm while wearing provocative costumes. Prominent dancers from the era included figures such as la Goulue, Jane Avril, la Môme Fromage, Grille d'Egout, Nini Pattes en l'Air, Yvette Guilbert, Valentin le désossé, and the clown Cha-U-Kao.

script_body: Under the German occupation, the Moulin Rouge kept its lights on. The German Occupation Guide listed it as a must-visit attraction, and its stage shows played on for the occupation troops — mentioned in the autobiographies of German officers such as Ernst Jünger and Gerhard Heller. The army ran 'recreational visits' to Paris for its soldiers under the motto 'Jeder einmal in Paris' — everyone once in Paris. The widespread prostitution of those years eventually brought the Loi Marthe Richard of 1946, which closed the bordellos and reduced the cabaret's stage shows to dancing events.

The Germans facilitated "recreational visits" in Paris for their troops, promoting the motto "Jeder einmal in Paris" (everyone once in Paris). script_body: The Grand Palais was built for a party: the Universal Exposition of 1900. Construction began in 1897, after the old Palais de l'Industrie — the Palace of Industry — was demolished to clear the ground, and the same exposition gave Paris the neighbouring Petit Palais and the Pont Alexandre III. It was conceived as a large-scale venue for official artistic events, and a pediment on the façade still declares its purpose: its inscription reads, 'a monument dedicated by the Republic to the glory of French art.' Designed to Beaux-Arts taste, it married ornate stone façades with glass vaults and the new techniques of the age — iron and light steel framing and reinforced concrete.

physical_cues.cue: The pediment inscription: 'a monument dedicated by the Republic to the glory of French art'

That exposition also produced the adjacent Petit Palais and Pont Alexandre III. The building was designed to be a large-scale venue for official artistic events. A pediment on the building refers to this function with an inscription that reads, "a monument dedicated by the Republic to the glory of French art." Designed according to Beaux-Arts tastes, the building features ornate stone facades, glass vaults and period innovations that included iron and light steel framing and reinforced concrete.

The main space was originally connected to the other parts of the palace along an east–west axis by a grand staircase in a style combining Classical and Art Nouveau, but the interior layout has since been somewhat modified.

The one on the Champs-Élysées side depicts Immortality prevailing over Time; the one facing the Seine depicts Harmony triumphing over Discord. Below them, the exterior sets an imposing Classical stone façade against a riot of Art Nouveau ironwork, studded with allegorical statue groups by sculptors including Paul Gasq, Camille Lefèvre, Alfred Boucher, Alphonse-Amédée Cordonnier and Raoul Verlet.

script_body: The Grand Palais has fought its own ground since the day it was built. Subsidence from a falling water table cracked the structure before it was even completed, and once it was in use, further damage piled on: heavy exhibitions strained the frame, and acid runoff from the horse shows ate at the metal. Differential expansion between cast iron and steel members let water enter, corroding the structure further. Finally, when one of the glass ceiling panels fell in 1993, the main space had to be closed for restoration, and was not fully reopened to the public until 2007.

Further damage occurred once the building was in use. Excessive force applied to structural members during the installation of certain exhibitions such as the Exposition Internationale de la Locomotion Aérienne caused damage, as did acid runoff from the horse shows. Differential rates of expansion and contraction between cast iron and steel members, for example, allowed for water to enter, leading to corrosion and further weakening. When finally one of the glass ceiling panels fell in 1993, the main space had to be closed for restoration work, and was not fully reopened to the public until 2007.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; subsidence + 1993 glass-panel fall + closure to 2007 documented

script_body: In World War II the building changed hands with the fighting. The Nazis used it first as a truck depot and then for two propaganda exhibitions; but during the Liberation of Paris the Parisian resistance made it a headquarters. On 23 August 1944, an advancing German column was fired upon from a window on the Avenue de Sèlves, and the Germans answered with a tank attack on the Palais. The shellfire set alight hay laid out for a circus show, and for the next forty-eight hours thick black smoke poured through the building, doing serious damage. By 26 August, American jeeps stood in the nave, followed by tanks of the French 2nd Armored Division, completing the liberation of the building.
source_passage: The Nazis put the Palais to use during the Occupation of France in World War II. First used as a truck depot, the Palais then housed two Nazi propaganda exhibitions. The Parisian resistance used the Grand Palais as a headquarters during the Liberation of Paris. On 23 August 1944, an advancing German column was fired upon from a window on the Avenue de Sèlves, and the Germans responded with a tank attack upon the Palais. The attack ignited hay that was set up for a circus show, and over the next 48 hours, thick black smoke from the fire caused serious damage to the building. By 26 August, American jeeps were parked in the nave, followed by tanks from the French 2nd Armored Division, completing the liberation of the building.

fact_check.omission_check: Core narrative corroborated (23 Aug 1944 German fire on the Resistance-held Grand Palais; 2nd Armored Division by 26 Aug). The circus-hay detail is specific to the Grand Palais article (it housed a circus during the occupation).

script_body: The Grand Palais came surprisingly close to being torn down. In the 1960s the architect Le Corbusier wanted it demolished and replaced with a Museum of 20th Century Art, a commission André Malraux had entrusted to him. Le Corbusier's death, on 27 August 1965, put an end to the project.

script_body: When restorers set out to find the metalwork's original colour, decades of overpainting had left it close to gray by 2001. Luck held: the company that supplied the paint in 1900, Ripolin, was still in business and still kept its archives. The records revealed the original shade — a 'Réséda' green, and specifically the palest of its three tones, 'pale reseda green.'
source_passage: As time took its toll, numerous layers of paint covered all the elements. The color visible in 2001 was close to gray. Luck is on the cards, as the manufacturer who supplied the paint in 1900 is still in business. This is the Ripolin company, which still has archives from the period in question. The corresponding color chart is quickly found, and the name of the color used is revealed: a "Réséda" green, of which there are three shades : pale, medium, and dark. The previous analyses clearly indicate the use of "pale reseda green."

fact_check.omission_check: Color corroborated: independent source describes the nave steelwork as 'mignonette green' (mignonette = reseda). Ripolin-archive specifics are single-source (the Wikipedia article) but plausible and uncontradicted.

script_body: The Grand Palais you can visit now is freshly restored. In October 2024, after four years of closure, it returned to the public and welcomed art fairs again, including Art Basel. The full reopening came in June 2025, at the end of a €466 million, four-year overhaul: its iconic glass roof restored, galleries improved, a new public entrance added, forty lifts installed, and a 'Children's Palace' created for young visitors. The work increased the building's capacity by 140 percent.

script_body: The Opéra Bastille is Paris's modern opera house, facing the Place de la Bastille. It was inaugurated in 1989 as part of President François Mitterrand's Grands Travaux — his great programme of monument-building — and became the main facility of the Paris National Opera, sharing the company with the older Palais Garnier; most opera performances are staged here, along with some ballet and symphony concerts. It was designed by the Uruguayan-Canadian architect Carlos Ott. With a main theatre, a concert hall and a studio theatre, it seats 2,723 people in all, making it the largest opera house in Europe.

Designed by Uruguayan-Canadian architect Carlos Ott, it is situated facing Place de la Bastille. It can seat 2,723 people in total, with a main theatre, concert hall and studio theatre, making it the largest opera house in Europe.

script_body: The architect was chosen by blind competition. An international contest drew 756 entries, and in November 1983 it was won by a little-known architect named Carlos Ott, an Uruguayan living in Canada. The jury, judging the designs without knowing who had made them, was said to have assumed this one came from the distinguished American architect Richard Meier — only to find the unknown Ott behind it. Construction began the next year, in 1984, on the site of the old gare de la Bastille, a train station that had opened in 1859 and closed in 1969.

It was said that the jury, who—as it is common with architectural competitions—did not know the names or track-records of the entrants, mistakenly assumed the design was by the distinguished American architect Richard Meier. Construction began in 1984 with the demolition of the gare de la Bastille train station, which had opened in 1859 and closed in 1969, and where art expositions had been held thereafter.

The opening gala was a semi-staged concert titled 'la Nuit avant le jour' — The Night Before the Day — directed by Robert Wilson and conducted by Georges Prêtre, with singers including Teresa Berganza and Plácido Domingo. The house was in fact unfinished that night: its first full opera, Hector Berlioz's 'les Troyens,' was not staged until 17 March 1990.

script_body: Even before it opened, the Opéra Bastille was engulfed in scandal. In 1987 the conductor Daniel Barenboim was hired as its first Artistic Director, but in January 1989 — six months before the inauguration — he was fired by the company's board chairman Pierre Bergé, head of the Yves Saint Laurent fashion house. Bergé reportedly objected to Barenboim's refusal to cut his pay by half, and to a modernist stance he deemed unfit for a 'popular' opera house. The artistic world erupted: Patrice Chéreau withdrew from staging the inaugural gala, Pierre Boulez resigned from the board, and Herbert von Karajan and Georg Solti signed a letter of protest and called for a boycott. In Barenboim's place, Bergé appointed a young and practically unknown Korean conductor, Myung-whun Chung.
source_passage: In 1987, conductor Daniel Barenboim, who had previously led the orchestre de Paris, was hired to become the house's first Artistic Director, and began planning the first seasons. In January 1989, six months before inauguration, the company's board chairman Pierre Bergé, otherwise head of the Yves Saint Laurent fashion house, fired Barenboim, reportedly after the conductor's refusal to cut his pay by half as well as due to his modernist stance, which Bergé deemed unfit for a "popular" opera house. This decision proved extremely controversial in the artistic field: Patrice Chéreau backed off the staging of the inaugural gala, composer Pierre Boulez resigned from the Board of Directors, and Herbert von Karajan and Georg Solti, along with several other prominent conductors, signed a letter of protest and called for a boycott of the opéra Bastille, canceling their own concerts there. In May, Bergé was finally able to announce the appointment of Korean pianist and conductor Myung-whun Chung, then young and practically unknown in France.

script_body: As early as 1991, some of the 36,000 Burgundy limestone panels covering the building began to fall. script_body: Inside, the auditorium makes a political point. Designed with 2,723 seats — later trimmed to 2,703 — it is laid out as an arena, a conscious, egalitarian departure from the Palais Garnier, whose several dozen types of seats leave many places without a view of the stage. Here every seat is the same type, with the same comfort and an unrestricted view of the stage, and there are no boxes. There is no royal or presidential box; instead the president's seat is simply a regular one in the arena, on the 'VIP' row, row 15, just after the central aisle — though not all presidents since 1989 have been avid opera-goers.
source_passage: The theatre's auditorium was designed with 2,723 seats, later reduced to 2,703. It is organised in an arena format with two huge balconies at the back, with a few narrow balconies on the sides. It was a conscious, egalitarian, departure from the Palais Garnier, which has several dozen types of seats and does not offer stage visibility from all of them. Every seat at the Opéra Bastille offers an unrestricted view of the stage, it is the very same type of seat with the same level of comfort, and there are no boxes. There is no "royal" or "presidential box"; instead, one of the regular seats in the arena, on the "VIP" row (row 15) just after the central aisle, is considered the presidential seat, although not all Presidents since 1989 have been avid opera-goers.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; 2,723 seats (later 2,703), arena format, no boxes, presidential seat is a regular row-15 seat

script_body: The Opéra Bastille is a machine as much as a building. The floor of its orchestra pit is actually an elevator, raised for a smaller orchestra and lowered for a larger, louder one; at its biggest it holds 130 players. Behind the stage lies an enormous backstage of 5,000 square metres — six times the size of the stage itself — with identical areas to the left, right and rear. A system of rails and a rotating dock can roll entire sets on and off on giant motorised platforms in a few minutes, while a giant elevator under the stage lowers unused sets to an underground storehouse as large as the backstage. It lets the company rehearse one work in the afternoon and perform another the same evening.
source_passage: One technical feature destined to make it better is that the floor of the orchestra pit is actually a small elevator, which makes it possible to adapt the pit to the requirements of the performance, elevating it for a smaller orchestra and lowering it for a larger and louder one; in its largest configuration, the pit has room for 130 players. The backstage occupies an enormous area (5,000 m2), six times larger than the stage: the stage area is flanked left and right with areas of the same size, and these three areas are replicated towards the back of the theatre. A system of rails and a rotating dock make it possible to roll entire sets on and off on giant motorised platforms in a few minutes and to store these platforms on the available backstage spots; quick changes of set enable the artists to rehearse a work in the afternoon and to perform another one in the evening within the same space. Under the stage is a giant elevator, which is used to lower unused set platforms to an underground storehouse as large as the backstage itself.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; elevator pit (up to 130 players) and 5,000 sqm backstage with rail/rotating-dock set storage documented

script_body: The tall column at the centre of the Place de la Bastille is the July Column, the Colonne de Juillet. It commemorates the Revolution of 1830 — the Trois Glorieuses, the 'three glorious days' of 27 to 29 July. Those three days toppled King Charles X and brought in the July Monarchy of Louis-Philippe. The column went up between 1835 and 1840.

source_passage: The July Column (French: Colonne de Juillet, [kɔlɔn d(ə) ʒɥijɛ]) is a monumental column in Paris commemorating the Revolution of 1830. It stands in the center of the Place de la Bastille and celebrates the Trois Glorieuses — the 'three glorious' days of 27–29 July 1830 that saw the fall of Charles X, King of France, and the commencement of the July Monarchy of Louis-Philippe, King of the French. It was built between 1835 and 1840.

script_body: This spot has carried monuments that never quite happened. As early as 1792, a column to commemorate the Fall of the Bastille was planned, and a foundation stone was laid on 14 July 1792 — but the project went no further. Under the Empire, the circular basin the column now stands in was built as part of the Elephant of the Bastille — a fountain with an elephant at its centre, finished in semi-permanent stucco. Its designer, the architect Jean-Antoine Alavoine, would himself later design the July Column. The permanent bronze version was never commissioned, the Empire's finances having run thin in its last days. The elephant's low base, however, was kept — and it still supports the socle — the column's footing.

physical_cues.cue: The circular basin and low base — once the Elephant of the Bastille — supporting the column

source_passage: A first project for one commemorative column, one that would commemorate the Fall of the Bastille, had been envisaged in 1792, and a foundation stone was laid, 14 July 1792; but the project never got further than that. The circular basin in which its socle stands was realised during the Empire as part of the Elephant of the Bastille, a fountain with an elephant in its centre. The elephant was completed to designs by Percier and Fontaine in semi-permanent stucco, but the permanent bronze sculpture was never commissioned due to pinched finances in the latter days of the Empire. Its low base has been retained to support the socle of the column.

fact_check.omission_check: Core confirmed: Empire-era Elephant of the Bastille fountain, stucco model erected 1814, permanent bronze never finished, base reused for the column.

corrections.original_text: completed to designs by Percier and Fontaine in semi-permanent stucco
corrections.corrected_text: completed in semi-permanent stucco to designs by the architect Jean-Antoine Alavoine — who would himself later design the July Column
corrections.reasoning: The Elephant of the Bastille is attributed to architect Jean-Antoine Alavoine (with sculptor Pierre-Charles Bridan), not Percier and Fontaine; the latter appears only in the July Column article and is an error. Alavoine also designed the July Column.

script_body: The monument inspired great music. For the laying of the first stone, a hymn with words by Victor Hugo and music by Ferdinand Hérold was sung at the Panthéon. And for the inauguration in 1840, Hector Berlioz composed his Grande Symphonie funèbre et triomphale, performing it in the open air himself as he led a procession of musicians that ended at the Place de la Bastille.

The Colonne de Juillet was constructed by Alavoine's partner in the project, Joseph-Louis Duc. It was inaugurated 28 July 1840. Music composed for the occasion was Hector Berlioz's Grande Symphonie funèbre et triomphale, which was performed in the open air under the direction of Berlioz himself, leading the procession of musicians which ended at the Place de la Bastille.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; Berlioz's Grande Symphonie funebre et triomphale first performed 28 Jul 1840 for the column's inauguration, military-band procession

script_body: The column is also a tomb. In its foundation, a columbarium — a vault of burial niches — holds the remains of 615 people killed in the July Revolution of 1830. Later, 200 victims of the Revolution of 1848 were laid there too — and in July 1848 the throne of Louis-Philippe, the very king who had raised the column, was symbolically burned in the square below it.

script_body: The column itself is built from twenty-one cast-bronze drums, weighing more than 74 tonnes and rising 47 metres high, with a spiral staircase hidden inside. It rests on a base of white marble ornamented with bronze bas-reliefs — carved panels — the most celebrated being the lion by the sculptor Antoine-Louis Barye, who also made the roosters at the corners. And around the shaft, engraved in gold, run the names of those who died in the July 1830 revolution.

The roosters at the corners are also by Barye. The column is engraved in gold with the names of those who died during the July 1830 revolution.

No claim added or strengthened.
fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; 21 bronze drums, 47m, spiral stair, Barye lion/roosters, gold-engraved names of the 1830 dead

script_body: Look to the very top. Above the Corinthian capital sits a gallery nearly five metres wide, crowned by a gilded globe, and on that globe stands the column's glory: a colossal gilded figure, the Génie de la Liberté — the 'Spirit of Freedom' — by the sculptor Auguste Dumont. Balanced on one foot in the manner of Giambologna's Mercury, the star-crowned nude figure brandishes the torch of civilisation and the remains of his broken chains. The figure once appeared on French ten-franc coins, and Gustave Flaubert, in Sentimental Education, compared it to a large golden star shining in the east.

script_body: The column was the work of the architect Jean-Antoine Alavoine, who shaped it as an elaborate Corinthian column on a commission from Louis-Philippe. The Place de la Bastille was officially selected as the site on 9 March 1831, and the Citizen-King laid the first stone on 28 July 1831 — the anniversary of the revolution that brought him to power. Alavoine's partner, Joseph-Louis Duc, carried the work through, and the finished column was inaugurated on 28 July 1840.

The Colonne de Juillet was constructed by Alavoine's partner in the project, Joseph-Louis Duc. It was inaugurated 28 July 1840.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; Alavoine then Duc, first stone 28 Jul 1831, inaugurated 28 Jul 1840

script_body: You are in the largest public park in Paris. The Bois de Vincennes spreads across the eastern edge of the city, created between 1855 and 1866 by the Emperor Napoleon III. It sits beside the Château de Vincennes, a former residence of the Kings of France, and packs in an astonishing variety: an English landscape garden with four lakes, a zoo, an arboretum, a botanical garden, a hippodrome for horse-racing, a velodrome for cycling, and the campus of France's national institute of sport and physical education.

physical_cues.cue: The wooded expanse of the park and the Château de Vincennes alongside it

source_passage: The Bois de Vincennes (French pronunciation: [bwɑ d(ə) vɛ̃sɛn]), located on the eastern edge of Paris, France, is the largest public park in the city. It was created between 1855 and 1866 by Emperor Napoleon III. The park is next to the Château de Vincennes, a former residence of the Kings of France. It contains an English landscape garden with four lakes; a zoo; an arboretum; a botanical garden; a hippodrome or horse-racing track; a velodrome for bicycle races; and the campus of the French national institute of sports and physical education.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; largest park in Paris, created 1855-1866 by Napoleon III

script_body: Just how big is it? The Bois de Vincennes covers 995 hectares — about a tenth of the entire area of Paris, and almost as much ground as the city's first six arrondissements combined. It is about three times larger than New York's Central Park, and slightly larger than London's Richmond Park. Only about half of it, though, is actually covered with trees.
source_passage: It occupies ten percent of the total area of Paris, and is almost as large as the first six arrondissements in the center of the city combined. The Bois de Vincennes is about three times larger than Central Park in New York City (341 hectares / 843 acres), and is slightly larger than Richmond Park in London (955 hectares / 2,360 acres); but is smaller than Griffith Park in Los Angeles (1,170 hectares / 2891 acres). Only about half of the Bois de Vincennes is covered with trees.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; 995 ha, ~3x Central Park, ~10% of Paris confirmed

script_body: Long before it was a park, this was a royal hunting forest. It was once part of the ancient woods around the Roman town of Lutetia, where it bore the name Vilcena — the origin of 'Vincennes.' Around 1150 King Louis VII built a hunting lodge here, on the site of the present château; King Philippe-Auguste later enclosed the forest with a wall, stocked it with game and began a castle. King Louis IX — Saint Louis — built a chapel beside it to house a relic he believed to be the crown of thorns from the Crucifixion. He was also famous for holding a royal court of justice under an oak near the château.
source_passage: The Bois de Vincennes was part of the ancient forest that surrounded the ancient Roman town of Lutetia; at that time it was called Vilcena, the origin of the present name. In about 1150 King Louis VII (1137–1180) built a hunting lodge at the site of the present chateau. King Philippe-Auguste (1180–1223) enclosed the forest with a wall, stocked it with game, and began building a castle. King Louis IX, or Saint Louis (1226–1270) built a chapel next to the castle to house an important religious relic, which he believed to be the crown of thorns from the Crucifixion of Jesus. He was also famous for holding a royal court of justice under an oak near the chateau.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; Vilcena etymology, Louis VII lodge, Philippe-Auguste wall, Saint Louis's oak court of justice are documented royal history

script_body: It was King Louis XV who first opened the forest to the public in the eighteenth century — to everyone, that is, except servants in livery. He had hundreds of trees planted and laid out long straight alleys through the woods in the form of intersecting stars, and in 1731 he built a pyramid-shaped monument to mark the meeting point of the two main alleys. It can still be seen.

source_passage: In the 18th century Louis XV (1710–1774) opened the park to the public, excepting servants in livery. He had hundreds of trees planted and laid out long straight alleys through the forest in the form of intersecting stars. In 1731 he constructed a pyramid-shaped monument to mark the meeting point of the two main alleys, which can still be seen.
