script_body: The Bois de Vincennes became a public park as part of Haussmann's remaking of Paris. In 1854 the Emperor Louis Napoleon and his new Prefect of the Seine, Georges-Eugène Haussmann, decided to transform it — and its purpose was pointedly social. It was to give green space and recreation to the large working-class population of eastern Paris, just as the Bois de Boulogne, begun in 1852, served the more affluent population of the west. To build it, Haussmann set up a new Service of Promenades and Plantations in 1855, led by the engineer Jean-Charles Adolphe Alphand — the great park-builder of nineteenth-century Paris, who also created Parc Monceau and the Parc des Buttes Chaumont.
source_passage: In 1854 the Emperor Louis Napoleon, and his new Prefect of the Seine, Georges-Eugène Haussmann, decided to transform the Bois de Vincennes into a public park. The purpose of the park was to provide green space and recreation to the large working-class population of eastern Paris, similar to the Bois de Boulogne, which Louis Napoleon had begun building in 1852 for the more affluent population of the west side of Paris. To build the parks, in 1855 Haussmann created a new Service of Promenades and Plantations, led by an engineer, Jean-Charles Adolphe Alphand, who was already at work on the Bois de Boulogne. Alphand was a master organizer, the builder of the most famous Paris parks of the 19th century; besides the Bois de Boulogne and Bois de Vincennes, he built the gardens of the Champs-Élysées, the boulevard of the Paris Observatory, Parc Monceau and the Parc des Buttes Chaumont.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; Napoleon III + Haussmann 1854, Alphand engineer, intended for the working-class east

script_body: Lac Daumesnil, at the western end of the park, was designed like a romantic landscape painting, with two islands and sloping green lawns. Much of the park's picturesque architecture was the work of the city architect Gabriel Davioud, and his prettiest flourish stands here: the Temple of Love, a round Doric temple set on a promontory of the Isle de Reuilly, above an artificial grotto. The same island once held a Swiss chalet — taken from the Paris Universal Exposition of 1867 — along with a café, a bandstand and concession stalls, and a swinging suspension bridge connected the lake's two islands.

physical_cues.cue: The Temple of Love — a round Doric temple — on the Isle de Reuilly in Lac Daumesnil, above its artificial grotto

source_passage: Lake Daumesnil, designed like a romantic landscape painting, had two islands, and sloping green lawns. The park was also decorated with picturesque architecture, mostly designed by Gabriel Davioud, the city architect. His works included the grandstands of the hippodrome and the Temple of Love, a round doric temple which was placed on a promontory on the Isle de Reuilly in Lac Daumesnil, above an artificial grotto. On the same island was a Swiss chalet (taken from the Paris Universal Exposition of 1867), a cafe, a bandstand, and buildings for vendors and game concessions. A swinging suspension bridge connected the two islands in the lake.

script_body: Twice the park hosted France's colonial expositions — vast fairs staged to showcase the French empire. The first, in 1907, built six 'villages, complete with inhabitants,' from across the empire: an encampment of Tuaregs from North Africa, a farm from Sudan, a village of Kanaks from New Caledonia, and villages from Madagascar, French Indochina and the Congo; two million people came to see it. The far larger 1931 Colonial Exposition filled the park with pavilions, a Senegalese village complete with inhabitants, a zoo, and eight spectacular fountains fed from Lake Daumesnil. Several traces survive: the entrance gate still stands, the Palace of the Colonies became the Museum of the Arts of Africa and the Oceania, and the pavilion of Cameroon was preserved and turned into a Buddhist temple.
entities: Museum of the Arts of Africa and the Oceania

physical_cues.cue: Surviving traces of the colonial fairs — the entrance gate, the former Palace of the Colonies, and the Cameroon pavilion turned Buddhist temple

source_passage: In 1907, this garden became the site of the first Colonial Exposition held in Paris, designed to showcase the cultures and products of the French colonies. The exposition featured six villages, complete with inhabitants, from the different parts of the French Empire; an emcampment of Tuaregs from North Africa; a farm from Sudan; a village of Kanaks from New Caledonia; and villages from Madagascar, French Indochina, and the Congo. The Exposition was seen by two million visitors. It had pavilions from each colony and from other nations, cafes and theaters, a Senegalese village complete with inhabitants, and a zoo. The exposition featured eight spectacular fountains, fed with water from Lake Daumesnil. The entrance gate is still standing. After the Fair closed, the Palace of the Colonies became the Museum of the Arts of Africa and the Oceania. The pavilion of Cameroon was preserved and turned into a Buddhist temple and religious center.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; 1907 (2M visitors) and 1931 (~8M) colonial expositions with inhabited 'villages'; Cameroon pavilion survives as a Buddhist temple, Palace of the Colonies became the museum (now Palais de la Porte Doree)

script_body: The Paris Zoological Park — the Zoo of Vincennes — opened in 1934, inspired by the popular zoo of the 1931 Colonial Exposition. Modelled on the Tierpark Hagenbeck in Hamburg, it was revolutionary for its time: instead of cages, it set the animals on open plateaus separated from the public by moats. Its great landmark is a sixty-five-metre-high artificial mountain, home to a herd of mouflon, or wild sheep. Its concrete buildings, built to last only fifty years, crumbled in the 1980s; the zoo closed in 2008 for a major renovation and reopened in 2014.

physical_cues.cue: The sixty-five-metre-high artificial mountain at the zoo

source_passage: The Paris Zoological Park, also known as Zoo of Vincennes, was opened in 1934, inspired by the popular zoo of the 1931 Colonial Exposition. It was modelled upon the Tierpark Hagenbeck in Hamburg, and was revolutionary for its time for putting the animals in open plateaus separated from the public by moats rather than in cages. The most prominent feature is a sixty-five meter high artificial mountain, which is the home of a herd of mouflon, or wild sheep. The park suffered from the crumbling of its concrete buildings in the 1980s, since they had been built to last only fifty years. It was closed in 2008 for major renovation, and reopened in 2014.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; zoo opened 1934, 65m Grand Rocher with mouflon, Hagenbeck-style moats, closed 2008 reopened 2014 (Tschumi redesign)

script_body: During the First World War, the Dutch spy Mata Hari was imprisoned in the fortress of Vincennes and executed by firing squad in its moat, on 15 October 1917. Eyewitnesses reported that her hands were not bound and that she refused a blindfold. According to legend — though it is undocumented — she blew a kiss to the firing squad and remarked, 'What a strange custom you French have, to shoot people at dawn.'
source_passage: During the First World War, the Dutch spy Mata Hari was imprisoned in the fortress of Vincennes and executed by firing squad in the moat of the fortress on 15 October 1917. Eyewitnesses reported that her hands were not bound, and that she refused a blindfold. According to the legend (not documented), she is said to have blown a kiss at the firing squad, and to have said, "What a strange custom you French have, to shoot people at dawn."

script_body: In the park's eastern corner lies the Jardin tropical, opened in 1899 as a garden for studying tropical plants. Its ruined colonial pavilions — from the French Congo, French Guiana, French Indochina, Réunion and Tunisia — can still be found among the trees. And in 1916 something remarkable rose here: the first mosque built in France in more than a millennium, raised as part of a hospital complex that served Muslim soldiers. It was demolished only three years later, in 1919.

source_passage: The Jardin tropical de Paris, of 4.5 hectares, was originally the Colonial Experimental Garden, opened in 1899 to study tropical plants. The pavilions of the French Congo, French Guiana, French Indochina, Réunion, and Tunisia, mostly vandalized and in ruins, can still be seen, as well as vestiges of the old Indochinese garden. In 1916, the first-ever mosque built in France in more than a millennium was erected in the jardin tropical as part of a hospital complex that served Muslim soldiers. It was disaffected and demolished in 1919.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions; first mainland-France mosque since the 8th c., erected early 1916 in the colonial/tropical garden, demolished 1919; ruined colonial pavilions still present

script_body: On 15 April 2019, the fire broke out in the attic of Notre-Dame at 18:18. The smoke detectors signalled immediately, but the cathedral employee on duty did not summon the fire brigade — instead, he sent a cathedral guard to investigate. The guard was sent to the wrong location, the attic of the adjoining sacristy, and reported there was no fire. About fifteen minutes later the error was discovered. By the time the guard had climbed the three hundred steps to the cathedral attic, the fire was well advanced. The alarm system was not designed to automatically notify the fire brigade, which was finally summoned at 18:51 — more than half an hour after the alarm had begun sounding.

physical_cues.cue: The cathedral roof and flèche above — the 2019 fire began in the attic

key_claims: Fire began in the attic at 18:18 on 15 April 2019
Smoke detectors signalled but a cathedral guard was sent to the wrong attic first
Fire brigade was not summoned until 18:51, half an hour after the alarm
source_passage:
On 15 April, a fire destroys a large part of the roof and the flèche.

The fire broke out in the attic of the cathedral at 18:18, investigators concluded. The smoke detectors immediately signalled the fire to a cathedral employee, who did not summon the fire brigade but instead sent a cathedral guard to investigate. The guard was sent to the wrong location, to the attic of the adjoining sacristy, and reported there was no fire. About 15 minutes later the error was discovered and the guard's supervisor told him to go to the correct location. The fire brigade was still not notified. By the time the guard had climbed the 300 steps to the cathedral attic, the fire was well advanced. The alarm system was not designed to automatically notify the fire brigade, which was summoned at 18:51 after the guard had returned from the attic and reported a now-raging fire, and more than half an hour after the fire alarm had begun sounding. Firefighters arrived in less than ten minutes.

script_body: The flèche collapsed at 19:50, bringing down 750 tonnes of stone and lead. By that point the fire had spread to the north tower, where the eight bells were. Firefighters feared that if the bells fell, they could wreck the tower and endanger the structure of the whole cathedral. A team of twenty firefighters climbed the narrow stairway of the south tower, crossed to the north tower, lowered hoses to be connected to fire engines outside, and sprayed water on the fire beneath the bells. By 21:45, they had brought the fire under control. The main structure was intact — façade, towers, walls, buttresses and stained-glass windows all saved.

physical_cues.cue: Two stone bell towers at the west façade — the north tower held the eight bells firefighters fought to save

key_claims: Flèche collapsed at 19:50, 750 tonnes of stone and lead
Twenty firefighters climbed south tower, crossed to north tower to save the bells
Fire under control by 21:45; main structure intact
source_passage: The cathedral's flèche collapsed at 19:50, bringing down 750 tonnes of stone and lead. The firefighters inside were ordered down. By this time the fire had spread to the north tower, where the eight bells were. The firefighters concentrated their efforts in the tower. They feared that, if the bells fell, they could wreck the tower, and endanger the structure of the other tower and the whole cathedral. They had to ascend a stairway threatened by fire, and to contend with low water pressure for their hoses. As others watered the stairway and the roof, a team of 20 firefighters climbed the narrow stairway of the south tower, crossed to the north tower, lowered hoses to be connected to fire engines outside the cathedral, and sprayed water on the fire beneath the bells. By 21:45, they brought the fire under control. The main structure was intact; firefighters saved the façade, towers, walls, buttresses, and stained-glass windows.

script_body: The fire of 15 April 2019 destroyed Notre-Dame's roof and its 19th-century flèche. On 16 December 2023, the new flèche was put in place, crowned with a gilded cockerel designed by architect Philippe Villeneuve. Inside the new cockerel are the same three relics the old one carried — a tiny piece from the Crown of Thorns, and relics of Saint Denis and Saint Genevieve, patron saints of Paris — placed there in 1935 by Archbishop Jean Verdier to protect the congregation from lightning. The cockerel also contains the names of two thousand people who participated in the reconstruction. To rebuild faithfully, Villeneuve's team scrutinised the journal in which Viollet-le-Duc had recorded every detail of his 19th-century work.

script_body: The construction of the Eiffel Tower was partly financed by the Crédit Industriel et Commercial — a French bank that was, at the same time, extracting predatory loans from Haiti. France had forced Haiti to compensate its former slaveowners for income lost to the Haitian Revolution, and required the country to pay CIC and its partner nearly half of all taxes collected on its exports. As The New York Times put it, while CIC was helping finance one of the world's best-known landmarks as a monument to French liberty, it was choking Haiti's economy, impairing the young nation's ability to build schools, hospitals and the other building blocks of independence.

source_passage: A French bank, the Crédit Industriel et Commercial (CIC), helped finance the construction of the Eiffel Tower. During the period of the tower's construction, the CIC was acquiring funds from predatory loans to the National Bank of Haiti, some of which went towards the financing of the tower. These loans were connected to an indemnity controversy that saw France force Haiti's government to financially compensate French slaveowners for lost income as a result of the Haitian Revolution, and required Haiti to pay the CIC and its partner nearly half of all taxes collected on exports, "effectively choking off the nation's primary source of income". According to The New York Times, "[at] a time when the [CIC] was helping finance one of the world's best-known landmarks, the Eiffel Tower, as a monument to French liberty, it was choking Haiti's economy, taking much of the young nation's income back to Paris and impairing its ability to start schools, hospitals and the other building blocks of an independent country."

script_body: On the day of the German occupation in 1940, the French cut the tower's lift cables; the lifts were not repaired until 1946. When the Allies were nearing Paris in August 1944, Hitler ordered General Dietrich von Choltitz, the military governor of the city, to demolish the tower along with the rest of Paris. Von Choltitz disobeyed. On 25 August, before the Germans had been driven out, two men from the French Naval Museum replaced the German flag with a Tricolour, narrowly beating three men led by Lucien Sarniguet — who, four years earlier, had lowered the Tricolour himself when Paris fell.

But in 1990, a French court ruled that the special lighting display installed for the tower's 100th anniversary was 'an original visual creation' protected by copyright, and the Court of Cassation upheld the ruling in 1992. The operating company now treats any illumination of the tower as a separate work of art under copyright. script_body: For most of the 19th century, the Arc was supposed to be crowned. Designs were proposed; in 1838 Bernard Seurre offered La France victorieuse — a chariot drawn by six horses; in 1840 Blouet installed a temporary group for the return of Napoleon's remains. The closest the monument ever came was from 1882 to 1886, when Alexandre Falguière hoisted up a plaster quadriga — Triomphe de la Révolution, a chariot of horses advancing 'to crush Anarchy and Despotism' — to test the visual effect. The effect was judged unconvincing. The piece stayed in place for four years anyway, the plaster softening under wind and rain, until it was finally removed. With that failure, the proposal to crown the Arc was abandoned for good. The flat top above you is the negative shape of an idea no one could ever make work.

key_claims: 1838: Bernard Seurre proposed La France victorieuse, a 6-horse chariot

Visual effect judged unconvincing; stayed 4 years as plaster deteriorated

source_passage:
Various designs were proposed to crown the monument with a monumental sculptural group, yet none was permanently realized. In 1838, Bernard Seurre submitted La France victorieuse ("Victorious France"), depicting a chariot drawn by six horses. In 1840, this proposal gave way to a temporary sculptural group representing Napoleon I, installed above the arch by the architect Guillaume-Abel Blouet for the return of the Emperor's remains. In preparing this installation, Blouet returned to a scheme he had drafted in 1834, modifying it by substituting the originally intended allegorical figure of France with that of the Emperor.
From 1882 to 1886, a quadriga by Alexandre Falguière was erected above the arch. The work, entitled Triomphe de la Révolution ("The Triumph of the Revolution"), depicted a chariot drawn by horses advancing "to crush Anarchy and Despotism". Executed in plaster, the group was hoisted to the summit of the monument in order to assess its visual effect. The result was judged unconvincing; although the sculpture remained in place for four years, its material deteriorated under exposure to the elements and it was ultimately removed. Following this episode, the proposal to crown the monument was ultimately abandoned.

script_body: Before 1920, victorious armies marched through the Arc. After the Unknown Soldier was interred beneath it, the custom changed: all parades go up to the Arc and then around its side, out of respect for the tomb. When the Germans entered Paris in 1940, Hitler observed the custom. When the Allies returned in 1944, Charles de Gaulle observed the same. The dead man under the stone has outranked every conqueror since.

source_passage: Following its construction, the Arc de Triomphe became the rallying point of French troops parading after successful military campaigns and for the annual Bastille Day military parade. Famous victory marches around or under the Arc have included the Germans in 1871, the French and Allies in 1919, the Germans in 1940, and the French and Allies in 1944 and 1945. After the interment of the Unknown Soldier, however, all military parades (including the aforementioned post-1919) have avoided marching through the actual arch. The route taken is up to the arch and then around its side, out of respect for the tomb and its symbolism. Both Adolf Hitler in 1940 and Charles de Gaulle in 1944 observed this custom.

script_body: In 1882 the walls of this basilica were barely above the foundations when Georges Clemenceau and his left-wing coalition won the parliamentary elections. Clemenceau proposed halting the work, and parliament blocked all further funding. But the government faced liabilities of twelve million francs from cancellation — more than the work itself had cost so far — and had to let construction proceed. Fifteen years later, in 1897, Clemenceau tried again. His motion was overwhelmingly defeated: by then, cancelling the project would have required repaying thirty million francs to the eight million people who had contributed.

During construction, opponents of the basilica were relentless in their effort to hinder its progress. In 1882, the walls of the church were barely above its foundations when the left-wing coalition led by Georges Clemenceau won the parliamentary election. Clemenceau immediately proposed halting the work, and the parliament blocked all further funding for the project. However, faced with enormous liabilities of twelve million francs from project cancellation, the government had to allow the construction to proceed.
In 1891, the interior of the basilica was completed, dedicated and opened for public worship. Still, in 1897, Clemenceau made another attempt to block its completion in the parliament, but his motion was overwhelmingly defeated since the cancellation of the project would require repaying thirty million francs to eight million people who had contributed to its construction.

script_body: The basilica's bid for monument historique status was caught in older politics. In 2021 — the 150th anniversary year of the Paris Commune — leftist members of parliament blocked the designation to avoid celebrating the church in that same year, and postponed the vote to 2022. On 8 December 2022, the National Commission of Patrimony and Architecture unanimously voted the church a national historic monument. The leftist politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon immediately called the vote 'a glorification of the assassination of 32,000 Paris Communards shot in just 8 days.'

This decision was immediately criticized by the leftist politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who called it "a glorification of the assassination of 32,000 Paris Communards shot in just 8 days".

script_body: The Savoyarde — the basilica's huge nineteen-tonne bourdon, the biggest bell in France — only rings on major religious holidays. Once it broke that rule. On the night of 24 August 1944, La Nueve — the 9th Company of the Régiment de marche du Tchad of the French 2nd Armored Division — reached the Hôtel de Ville, the first French Army troops to return to Paris since 1940. Pierre Schaeffer broadcast the news on Radiodiffusion Nationale, played La Marsellaise over the air, and asked any priest who was listening to ring his church's bells. The Savoyarde rang. It can be heard from ten kilometres away.

script_body: The basilica's grand organ was the last instrument ever built by Aristide Cavaillé-Coll, the 19th century's most celebrated Paris organ-builder. It was built in 1898 for the Biarritz chateau of Baron Albert de L'Espée. It had a twin — tonally identical, with the same layout and the same casework — installed in Sheffield's Albert Hall, which was destroyed by fire in 1937. The Sacré-Cœur organ was installed in Paris in 1905 by Cavaillé-Coll's son-in-law, Charles Mutin, but a much plainer case was substituted for the original ornate one.

The basilica contains a large and very fine pipe organ built by Aristide Cavaillé-Coll, the most celebrated organ builder in Paris in the 19th century.
The organ was originally built in 1898 for the Biarritz chateau of the Baron Albert de L'Espée. It was the last instrument built by Cavaillé-Coll. The organ was ahead of its time, containing multiple expressive divisions and giving the performer considerable advantages over other even larger instruments of the day. It was almost identical (tonal characteristics, layout, and casework) to the instrument in Sheffield's Albert Hall, which was destroyed by fire in 1937. However, when installed in Paris in 1905 by Cavaillé-Coll's successor and son-in-law, Charles Mutin, a much plainer case was substituted for the original ornate case.

In 1978, a competition was organized to design the new museum. ACT Architecture, a team of three young architects (Pierre Colboc, Renaud Bardon and Jean-Paul Philippon), were awarded the contract which involved creating 20,000 square metres (220,000 sq ft) of new floorspace on four floors. The construction work was carried out by Bouygues. In 1981, the Italian architect Gae Aulenti was chosen to design the interior including the internal arrangement, decoration, furniture and fittings of the museum. The arrangement of the galleries she designed was elaborate and inhabited the three main levels that are under the museum's barrel vault atrium. On the main level of the building, a central nave was formed by the surrounding stone structures that were previously the building's train platforms. The central nave's structures break up the immense sculpture and gallery spaces and provided more organized units for viewing the art.
In July 1986, the museum was ready to receive its exhibits. It took 6 months to install the 2,000 or so paintings, 600 sculptures and other works. The museum officially opened in December 1986 by then-president François Mitterrand.

As the status of Saint Louis grew among Europe's aristocracy, the influence of his famous chapel also extended beyond France, with important copies at Karlštejn Castle near Prague (c. 1360), the Hofburgkapelle in Vienna (consecrated 1449), Collegiate Church of the Holy Cross and St. Bartholomew, Wrocław (c. 1350) and Exeter College, Oxford (1860).

script_body: The names of the master glaziers who built these windows between 1242 and 1248 have all been lost. But art historian Louis Grodecki identified three different workshops by style. The first made the apse windows and most of the north wall — supple forms, simplified features. The second, the Master of the Ezekiel Window, made the Ezekiel, Daniel and Kings windows — elongated figures, angular drapery. The third, the Master of Judith and Esther, made those two windows and the window of Job — subtler faces, the feel of an illuminated manuscript.

The names of the glass artists are unknown, but the art historian Louis Grodecki identified what appear to be three different ateliers with different styles. The windows in the apse and most of the windows on the north wall of the nave are made by one workshop. These works are known for supple forms and costumes, with simplified features. The second workshop, named by Grodecki as Master of the Ezekiel window, made the Ezekiel and Daniel windows, as well as the window of the Kings. That work is characterized by elongated forms, and more elaborate and angular draperies. The third artist or workshop is called the Master of Judith and Esther, for the distinct style of those windows, as well as the window of Job. They are distinguished by more subtle details in the faces, and a resemblance to the figures in illuminated manuscripts.

script_body: Empress Eugénie had wanted Viollet-le-Duc to win the commission. When Garnier — relatively unknown — was chosen instead, she confronted him over the new style. Legend has it she said: 'What is this? It's not a style; it's neither Louis Quatorze, nor Louis Quinze, nor Louis Seize!' Garnier replied: 'Why Ma'am, it's Napoléon Trois — and you're complaining!' The historian Andrew Ayers has called Garnier's label undisputed: the Palais Garnier so perfectly captured the Second Empire — a giddy mixture of up-to-the-minute technology, prescriptive rationalism, exuberant eclecticism, and astonishing opulence — that the style and the building share a name.

A giddy mixture of up-to-the-minute technology, rather prescriptive rationalism, exuberant eclecticism and astonishing opulence, Garnier's opera encapsulated the divergent tendencies and political and social ambitions of its era."

script_body: Three thousand vehicles an hour through eight lanes left the Champs-Élysées more polluted than the Périphérique itself — nitrogen-dioxide levels twice the WHO limit. Seventy-two percent of the hundred thousand pedestrians on the avenue each day in 2019 were tourists; another twenty-two percent worked there. Parisians had largely written the place off. In early 2021 the Mayor of Paris, Anne Hidalgo, announced a transformation: an 'extraordinary garden' — auto-traffic space halved, 'tunnels of trees' planted, more than 200 acres of green stretched between the Arc, Concorde and the Tuileries. The estimated bill was €250 million, and serious work was held off until after the 2024 Olympics.

The Champs-Élysées has encountered rising problems with air pollution from the estimated 3,000 vehicles per hour which drive through its eight lanes. It is more polluted than the Périphérique ring road which encircles the city, with nitrogen dioxide levels twice as high as the recommended limit set by the World Health Organization. Since 2016, the avenue has been closed to motor traffic on the first Sunday of every month, in an effort to cut pollution in the city. A 2019 article in The Guardian stated that the avenue "has more and more visitors and big name businesses battle to be on it, but to French people it's looking worn out." It has also become mainly a tourist attraction, which Parisians largely avoid. According to the architect Philippe Chiambaretta, 72% of the 100,000 pedestrians who visited the Champs-Élysées each day in 2019 were tourists and another 22% worked there.
At the beginning of 2021, the Mayor of Paris, Anne Hidalgo, announced that the city would transform the Champs-Élysées into an "extraordinary garden" which will reduce the space for auto traffic by half, add more pedestrian space, and create "tunnels of trees" for improved air quality. A walkway will connect over 200 acres of green space stretching between the Arc de Triomphe, the Place de la Concorde, and the Tuileries Gardens. The plans are meant to make the avenue more "ecological, desirable and inclusive," and will cost an estimated €250 million. It will include a redesign of the Place de la Concorde as well. The work did not begin in earnest until after the 2024 Summer Olympics held in Paris; the goal is to complete the project by 2030.

script_body: There is a claim that the Champs-Élysées owes part of its shape to a small English seaside town. In 1846, the future Napoleon III lived for a brief period in lodgings just off Lord Street in Southport. The street is said to have been an inspiration for what he would later do in Paris. Years on, in 1858, after he had become Emperor, his Prefect of the Seine, Georges-Eugène Haussmann, transformed the Champs-Élysées gardens from a formal French garden into a picturesque English-style garden — based explicitly on a small town called Southport — with winding paths, groves of trees, and the elms (in poor health by then) replaced with rows of chestnut trees.

script_body: When the guillotine first arrived in this square in October 1792, its first two victims were not aristocrats. They were two thieves who had stolen the royal crown diamonds from the Hôtel de la Marine on the north side. On 11 May 1793 the guillotine was set up again — midway between the Statue of Liberty and the turning bridge to the Tuileries — and stayed there for thirteen months. Of the 2,498 people guillotined in Paris during the Revolution, 1,119 died here, 1,306 at the Place de la Nation, and 73 at the Place de la Bastille. The last executions on the square were the Prairial riot participants, in May 1795.

script_body: Muhammad Ali Pasha, the wali of Egypt, offered France two obelisks in 1829. One — the Luxor Obelisk — was hauled from the Luxor Temple to Paris and hoisted into place on the old Louis XV pedestal on 25 October 1836. The other was simply too difficult to move with 19th-century technology and stayed at Luxor. On 26 September 1981, President François Mitterrand formally returned the title to Egypt — France was no longer the legal owner. In 1998, the French government added a gold-leafed pyramidal cap to the top of the Paris obelisk, replacing one believed to have been stolen in the 6th century BC.

script_body: The Revolutionary Tribunal moved in upstairs, in the Grand Chamber between the Silver and Caesar towers — renamed the 'Hall of Liberty'. Its public prosecutor, Antoine Quentin Fouquier-Tinville, set up his office and his residence next door. Trials were public, rapid, unappealable. The Law of Suspects on 17 September 1793 sent monthly executions from 11 to 124. On 10 June 1794 the law was tightened again — witnesses no longer required, 'suspect' enlarged — and by the end of that month an average of 38 people a day were tried, sentenced, and sent to the guillotine. Four out of five were condemned to die. In August 1794 Fouquier-Tinville himself was arrested. He spent nine months in this prison — pleading that 'the execution of the laws, justice and humanity were always my sole rules of conduct' — before going to the guillotine on 7 May 1795. In 780 days the Tribunal had sentenced and executed 2,780.

source_passage:
The Revolutionary Tribunal was created on March 10, 1793 by the more radical Montagnard faction over the opposition of the more moderate Girondins. The Tribunal met in the Grand Chamber of Palace on the upper floor between the Silver and Caesar towers. It was renamed the "Hall of Liberty." Antoine Quentin Fouquier-Tinville, a Montagnard, was named public prosecutor and installed his office and residence next to the Chamber. In September 1793, the Terror intensified. The National Convention, controlled by the Montagnards, enacted the Law of Suspects on September 17, 1793. The Tribunal had five judges and 12 selected jury members. Trials were public and rapid and attracted large crowds. Verdicts could not be appealed. The number of monthly executions grew from 11 a month before the Law of Suspects to 124 per month.
On June 10, 1794, the court procedure was modified to allow speedier trials, witnesses were no longer needed and the definition of "suspect" was enlarged. By the end of June, an average of 38 persons a day were being tried, sentenced and sent to the guillotine. Between 1793 and 1795, two-thirds of prisoners tried were sentenced to death. At the peak of the Reign of Terror, four out of five prisoners were sentenced to death,
In August, the head of the tribunal, Fouquier-Tinville, was arrested and tried. He argued that "the execution of the laws, justice and humanity were always my sole rules of conduct" but he was confined for nine months in the Conciergerie and went to the guillotine on May 7, 1795. The tribunal was abolished on May 31, 1795. In 780 days, the tribunal had sentenced and executed 2,780 prisoners.

Placed in the northwest corner, it was set slightly apart from the rest of the building, to reduce the risk of fire. It was originally installed on two levels, with the food of the royal family and guests prepared on the upper level, and for the staff on the lower level. When the king was in residence, meals were prepared in a large hearth on the upper floor, or prepared in the lower kitchen and taken upstairs on an outside ramp, no longer extant. Sometimes both the upper and lower kitchens were employed for an event, such as the Banquet of the Three Kings on 6 January 1378, held by Charles V to welcome his uncle, Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor, and his cousin Wenceslaus, King of the Romans. The upstairs and downstairs kitchens worked together to prepare a banquet of three courses with ten dishes in each course, served in the Grand Hall to the royal guests and to eight hundred German and French knights.

script_body: Even during the Terror, the Conciergerie ran a tariff. A wealthy prisoner could rent a bed for 27 livres 12 sous for the first month, 22 livres 10 sous after that — eventually dropped to 15. The prison commanders made a fortune. As the Terror escalated, a prisoner could pay for a bed, be guillotined a few days later, and free the bed for a new inmate who would then pay as well. One memoirist called the Conciergerie 'the most lucrative furnished lodgings in Paris.' For most prisoners, though, the cells were cramped, rat-infested, and stinking of urine, and the special privileges of the wealthy were largely cut as the Terror peaked.

script_body: The Tour de l'Horloge — completed in 1350 under John II — is the Conciergerie's tallest tower and Paris's oldest clock tower. Henri de Vic installed the mechanism here during the reign of Charles V: the first public clock in Paris. In 1585 Henry III dressed it up with a new face — gold fleurs-de-lis on a blue background, framed by statues of Law and Justice by Germain Pilon. The decoration was vandalised in the Revolution; the great bell, rung for major events, was taken down and melted. The tower was most recently restored in 2012.

source_passage: The most recent tower is the Tour de l'Horloge, or clock tower, at the corner of the Boulevard du Palais and the Quai de l'Horloge. It was completed by John II of France, and finished in 1350. It is the tallest tower of the Conciergerie, five levels high, with battlements and a lantern tower at the top; it served as both a watchtower and clock tower. The clock was made by Henri de Vic and installed during the reign of Charles V of France, and was the first public clock in Paris. In 1585 King Henry III of France embellished the clock with a new face, set on a blue background with gold fleurs-de-lis, and framed by statues of law and justice by sculptor Germain Pilon. The decoration was vandalised during the Revolution, and the large bell in the lantern, which was rung to celebrate major events, was taken out and melted down. The tower had been restored several times, most recently in 2012.

script_body: Louis Daguerre's 1838 daguerreotype of the Boulevard du Temple is the picture usually called the first photograph in which a human being can be seen. But two years earlier, between 1836 and 1837, Daguerre was running outdoor tests of his new technique — and one of those tests pointed at the Pont Neuf. It captured the bridge and the equestrian statue of Henry IV. On the lower-left of the image, in the shadow of the statue, what appears to be a worker — perhaps two — can be seen lying against the fence. If the dating holds, that figure may be the first human ever photographed.

script_body: Three hundred and eighty-one carved stone faces decorate the bridge — each one different from the others. They are heads of forest and field divinities from ancient mythology, plus satyrs and sylvains, copies of originals attributed to the French Renaissance sculptor Germain Pilon — who also carved the tomb of Henry II and Catherine de'Medici at Saint-Denis. The Pilon originals lasted until 1851-1854, when the bridge was completely rebuilt. Six were sent to the Musée Carnavalet, eight others to the Cluny — they are now at the Musée National de la Renaissance at Château d'Écouen. The new copies were carved by Hippolyte Maindron, Hubert Lavigne, Antoine-Louis Barye and Fontenelle — Fontenelle alone made 61, on the upstream side between the right bank and the Île de la Cité.

source_passage: The mascarons are 381 stone masks, each different from the others, which decorate the sides of the bridge. They represent the heads of forest and field divinities from ancient mythology, as well as satyrs and sylvains. They are copies of the originals attributed to the French Renaissance sculptor Germain Pilon (1525–1590), who also sculpted the tomb of King Henry II of France and Queen Catherine de'Medici in the Basilica of St Denis, five kilometers north of Paris. The mascarons remained in place until 1851–1854, when the bridge was completely rebuilt. At that time six of the original mascarons from the 16th century were placed in the Musée Carnavalet, along with eight molds of other originals. Eight other originals were first placed in the Musée de Cluny – Musée national du Moyen Âge, and are now in the French National Museum of the Renaissance in the Château d'Écouen. During their reconstruction, the Renaissance masks were replaced with copies made by noted 19th-century sculptors, including Hippolyte Maindron, Hubert Lavigne, Antoine-Louis Barye and Fontenelle. Fontenelle made 61 masks, which are found on the upstream side of the bridge between the right bank and the Île de la Cité.

script_body: Every year on the Petite Fête-Dieu — the 'Small Corpus Christi' eight days after the main feast — young painters showed their canvases on the Place Dauphine just off the bridge, between six in the morning and noon. It was an unofficial salon, an opportunity for unknowns to be noticed — a forerunner of the Salon des Refusés that would later spark the Impressionists. In 1720, a twenty-two-year-old, the son of the man who maintained the king's billiards, showed an antique bas-relief here. J.-B. Vanloo passed by, looked at the canvas for a long time, found great qualities there, bought it, and started looking after the young painter. Eight years later, that young painter was Vanloo's colleague at the Academy of Painting. His name was Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin.

script_body: The original equestrian statue of Henry IV at the heart of the bridge was destroyed in 1792. When the Bourbons returned, the statue was rebuilt in 1818 — by public subscription. Bronze for the new statue was obtained by melting down a statue of Louis Charles Antoine Desaix. The new cast was made from a surviving mould of the original. Before the new Henri IV was sealed, the sculptor François-Frédéric Lemot hid four boxes inside it: a history of the life of Henri IV, a 17th-century parchment certifying the original statue, a document describing how the new statue had been commissioned, and a list of the people who had contributed to the public subscription.

source_passage: At the point where the bridge crosses the Île de la Cité, there stands a bronze equestrian statue of king Henry IV, originally commissioned from Giambologna under the orders of Marie de Médicis, Henri's widow and Regent of France. After his death, Giambologna's assistant Pietro Tacca completed the statue, which was erected on its pedestal by Pietro Francavilla, in 1614. It was destroyed in 1792 during the French Revolution, but was rebuilt in 1818, following the restoration of the Bourbon monarchy. Commissioned from public donations, bronze for the new statue was obtained from a statue of Louis Charles Antoine Desaix and melted down. The new statue was cast from a mold made using a surviving cast of the original. Inside the statue, the new sculptor François-Frédéric Lemot put four boxes, containing a history of the life of Henry IV, a 17th-century parchment certifying the original statue, a document describing how the new statue was commissioned, and a list of people who contributed to a public subscription.

script_body: The island you are standing on is bigger than it used to be. Sandbar after sandbar accumulated, and then stone-faced embankments — the quais — locked the new ground into place. The original Roman wharf, built where the Parvis Notre-Dame is today, is now well inland. In 1607, when the Pont Neuf was completed, two small islands just to the west — the Île à la Gourdaine and the Île aux Juifs — were joined to the Cité. Together they became the Place Dauphine and the Square du Vert-Galant.

script_body: In the 3rd century AD, Germanic invasions hit Lutetia. The town on the left bank was sacked in 275-276. Afterwards, the left bank was largely abandoned. Beginning in 307, the city retreated to this island. The forum, the amphitheatre and the other structures of the left bank were demolished, and the stone was used to construct a rampart around the island — and to put up new buildings. The wall was not high, only about two metres, topped by a wooden palisade. But it made the island a defensive position on the Roman Empire's northern flank. In 451, when the Huns reached the left bank, Saint Genevieve led the defence of the city from here.

script_body: There is a quiet academic argument over whether the original Lutetia of the Gauls was really here. Between 1994 and 2005, archaeologists excavated a large Gallic necropolis — with residences and temples — at Nanterre, along the Seine in the Paris suburbs. Some historians have proposed Nanterre as the true Lutetia of the Gauls. Others point to Caesar's own description: 'Lutetia, fortress (oppidum) of the Parisii, situated on an island.' They argue that the absence of pre-Roman traces on the Île de la Cité is simply due to continuous building and rebuilding over the centuries — every previous layer ground up by the next one.

Some historians have put forward this settlement at Nanterre as the Lutetia of the Gauls, rather than Île de la Cité. Other historians point out that Caesar described "Lutetia, fortress ('oppidum') of the Parisii, situated on an island." They say that the absence of traces of pre-Roman settlement discovered so far on Île de la Cité is due primarily to the continuous building and rebuilding on the island over the centuries.

script_body: By the 14th century, the island was suffocating. Crowded streets, jammed traffic, pollution, foul smells — the everyday life of a medieval city compressed onto a few hectares of rock. The Kings of France started looking for a way out. In 1358, while Jean II was a hostage of the English, the merchants' provost Étienne Marcel led a rebellion of the Parisians right here, at the palace. That was the breaking point. Jean's successor Charles V moved his residence to the edge of the city — first to the Hôtel Saint-Pol, then to the Bastille, finally to the Louvre. The kings would not live on the island again.

In the mid-19th century, the island was overcrowded, with narrow streets and poor sanitation. It was hard hit by major cholera epidemics in 1832 and 1849, which killed thousands of Parisians. The new president, and then Emperor, Napoleon III, ordered the demolition of the old streets and buildings and the opening of wide avenues and squares. The Parvis in front of the cathedral was greatly increased in size. In 1867, Napoleon III also demolished the overcrowded medieval hospital, the Hôtel-Dieu, and replaced it with the present building.
The parvis or square in front of the cathedral – now officially known as Place Jean-Paul-II – is 135 metres (443 ft) long and 106 metres (348 ft) wide, six times larger than the original medieval square.

script_body: The island has had bridges since it was first inhabited. The early ones were wood: the Grand Pont (later the Pont au Change) to the right bank, the Petit Pont to the left. The first stone bridge to the island was built in 1378 at the site of today's Pont Saint-Michel. Thirty years later, in 1408, ice floes carried it away — along with all the houses on it. The Grand Pont and the Petit Pont, both swept away at intervals by floodwaters, were rebuilt by Fra Giovanni Giocondo at the beginning of the 16th century. Houses lined the Pont Notre-Dame's six arches until 1786, when they were all demolished. Eight bridges connect the island to the city today.

script_body: The memorial was designed by the modernist architect Georges-Henri Pingusson and inaugurated by President Charles de Gaulle on 12 April 1962. It honours the two hundred thousand people deported from Vichy France to the Nazi concentration camps. Pingusson shaped it like the prow of a ship and put it underground. A brochure produced by the French survivors' group Reseau de Souvenir in the year of its opening described it as a crypt 'hollowed out of the sacred isle, the cradle of our nation, which incarnates the soul of France — a place where its spirit dwells.' Pingusson designed the long, narrow subterranean chamber to feel claustrophobic — to convey what could not be said.

The Mémorial des martyrs de la Déportation (English: Memorial to the martyrs of the Deportation) is a memorial to the 200,000 people who were deported from Vichy France to the Nazi concentration camps during World War II. It is located in Paris, France, on the site of a former morgue, underground behind Notre Dame on Île de la Cité. It was designed by French modernist architect Georges-Henri Pingusson and was inaugurated by Charles de Gaulle in 1962.
Designed by French architect, writer, teacher, and town planner Georges-Henri Pingusson (1894–1978), the memorial was inaugurated by then-President Charles de Gaulle on April 12, 1962. In the year of its opening, a brochure produced by the French survivors' group "Reseau de souvenir" described the memorial as a crypt, "hollowed out of the sacred isle, the cradle of our nation, which incarnates the soul of France – a place where its spirit dwells."

script_body: The descent begins with two staircases and a lowered square sealed by a metal portcullis. Below is a hexagonal rotunda with two chapels holding earth and bones from the camps. The narrow entrance between two concrete blocks gives onto a long dim chamber. Inside that chamber lies the tomb of an unknown deportee — killed at Natzweiler-Struthof. Two hundred thousand small glass crystals are mounted along the walls of the corridor, each lit from behind, each representing a deportee who died in the camps. At the far end of the tunnel, a single bright light. At either lateral end, urns hold ashes from the camps. Opposite the entrance, a stark iron gate looks out over the Seine at the tip of the island.

poi_name: Memorial des Martyrs de la Deportation
script_body: On the walls inside are inscriptions by Louis Aragon, Paul Éluard, Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, Jean-Paul Sartre — and Robert Desnos, a French poet and Resistance member who was himself a deportee. Two of his poems are here. The first is the final stanza of 'À la mystérieuse', originally published in Corps et Biens in 1930. After Desnos died at Theresienstadt, his poem was translated into Czech — and then retranslated back into French in Les Lettres françaises in 1945. It begins: 'I have dreamt so very much of you, I have walked so much, Loved your shadow so much, That nothing more is left to me of you.' And ends: 'All that remains to me is to be the shadow among shadows, to be a hundred times more of a shadow than the shadow, to be the shadow that will come and come again into your sunny life.'

poi_name: Memorial des Martyrs de la Deportation
script_body: Architectural Digest put the memorial on its list of the 'Ten Most Significant Memorial Buildings' — 'rather than rising heroically, the memorial is meant to evoke the unspeakable, anonymous drama of deportation — its entrance a descending stairway.' A Guardian reader called it 'small, stark and savagely detailed... which goes unnoticed by the thousands of tourists who take selfies of themselves in front of the adjoining cathedral every day. It is a place for tears and quiet contemplation; a refuge from the crowds and a reminder of one of the darkest episodes in recent history.' Not everyone is satisfied. The historian Peter Carrier has criticised the memorial for lacking specific references to Jewish victims — the dedication to 'the two hundred thousand French martyrs', he argues, suggests they died willingly for a national cause rather than as victims of state persecution. His critique: that the memorial 'symbolically assimilates the specific Jewish memory of the Second World War into national memory.'

script_body: In 2002, Bertrand Delanoë — Paris's first openly gay mayor — threw open the long-inaccessible doors of the Hôtel de Ville for the first citywide Nuit Blanche. That same evening, inside, he was stabbed. He recovered. And he did not lose his zeal for access: he later turned the mayor's sumptuous private apartments into a crèche for the children of municipal workers.

script_body: Look up at the façade. Two hundred and thirty sculptors were commissioned to produce three hundred and thirty-eight individual statues of famous Parisians — lions and decorative figures alongside. Among the sculptors were academicians Ernest-Eugène Hiolle and Henri Chapu. The most famous of them was Auguste Rodin: his contribution, finished in 1882, is the figure of the eighteenth-century mathematician Jean le Rond d'Alembert. Allegorical figures of Art (by Laurent Marqueste) and Science (by Jules Blanchard) flank the central ceremonial doors under the clock.

script_body: On 30 October 1870, during the Franco-Prussian War, revolutionaries broke into the Hôtel de Ville and captured several members of the Government of National Defence, demanding that a communard government be established. The existing government escaped — through a tunnel built in 1807 that still connects the Hôtel de Ville to a nearby barracks. Three months later, on 23 January 1871, crowds gathered outside the building to protest the speculated surrender to the Prussians. Soldiers inside the Hôtel de Ville fired on them, killing several.

script_body: In 1533, Francis I decided his capital deserved a city hall worthy of it. Paris was then the largest city in Europe and Christendom. He appointed two architects: the Frenchman Pierre Chambiges, and the Italian Dominique de Cortone — nicknamed 'Boccador' for his red beard. The old House of Pillars was torn down, and Boccador, steeped in the Renaissance, drew up the plans for a building that was tall, spacious, full of light, and refined. The work wasn't finished for almost a century: not until 1628, under Louis XIII.

script_body: On 1 December 1783, the first free flight of a manned hydrogen balloon lifted off from the Tuileries. Jacques Alexandre César Charles and Nicolas Louis Robert went up. The King watched the flight from the tower of the palace. Benjamin Franklin, the first American ambassador to Paris, had attended the balloon's first trial in the garden. The balloon — and its passengers — landed safely thirty-one miles from Paris, at Nesles-la-Vallée.

script_body: For the 2024 Olympics, a platform was installed in the middle of the Grand Bassin Rond, carrying the city's Olympic and Paralympic cauldron. Mathieu Lehanneur designed it as the bottom of a hot-air balloon in tribute to the Montgolfier brothers — a thirty-metre helium sphere above a seven-metre ring of fire. It was the first Olympic cauldron in history to burn without using fossil fuels. The Olympic flame was lit on 28 July by judoka Teddy Riner and sprinter Marie-José Pérec, both native Guadeloupeans. By day the cauldron rested above the basin; at sunset and during the opening ceremonies it rose into the sky, anchored to the ground by a wire-like conduit. Up to ten thousand visitors a day came to see it during the Games. It returned to the basin in summer 2025 — flying weekends and public holidays, grounded but illuminated the rest of the week — and was scheduled to return every summer through 2027.

poi_name: Galerie nationale du Jeu de Paume
script_body: Built in 1861 under Napoleon III as an indoor tennis court — the original jeu de paume — and enlarged in 1878, the Galerie nationale du Jeu de Paume has worn three different lives. During the German occupation, it was used as a warehouse for art the Nazis had stolen or confiscated across France. After the war, from 1947 to 1986, it became the annex where the Louvre showed its Impressionist paintings — until those works were transferred to the new Musée d'Orsay. From the 1990s on, the gallery has shown contemporary art.

script_body: An English oak planted on the Esplanade des Feuillants in 1992 commemorates the 200th anniversary of the French Republic. It is a reminder of the Liberty Tree — a symbol that first appeared in America before the American Revolution, then planted around France during the Revolution. In the Revolution of 1848, Louis XVI himself planted the first liberty tree in the Tuileries Garden. After his execution, it was cut down. A stylised depiction of a Liberty Tree decorates the French one-euro and two-euro coins.

script_body: Monet's Water Lilies have hung here since 1927. During the German occupation, the Orangerie hosted an exposition of work by Arno Breker, Hitler's favourite sculptor. When Paris was liberated in 1944, heavy fighting through the gardens damaged Monet's paintings. Two years later, in 1946, the French Commission for Art Recovery and the Monuments Men brought masterpieces back from Germany, and the Orangerie became the staging ground where they were restored to their owners and their surviving families.

The Orangerie, originally used to keep citrus trees during the winter, was also made into a gallery, with the eastern wing devoted to the display of eight paintings of the Water Lilies series by Claude Monet. They were installed there in 1927, shortly after Monet's death.
